lessons.title: Der Schrank steht, ich stelle ihn: stehen or stellen?
lessons.goal: Decide between stehen (Wo? dative, no object) and stellen (Wohin? accusative, with object), use both in the Perfekt, and set up the free room.

grammar.topic: stehen or stellen: the object test
grammar.point: A verb that only says where a thing is (stehen) has no object and the two-way preposition takes the dative (Wo?). A verb that moves a thing (stellen) has an object and the preposition takes the accusative (Wohin?). Perfekt: hat gestanden, hat gestellt, hat aufgestellt.
grammar.oneLine: Der Schrank steht in der Ecke. Ben stellt den Schrank in die Ecke.

mistake.wrong: Ich stehe den Schrank in die Ecke.
mistake.right: Ich stelle den Schrank in die Ecke.
mistake.why: Stellen has an object (den Schrank) and answers Wohin?, so it takes the accusative. Stehen never has an object.

terms.meaning: is there an object that somebody moves? yes: stellen + accusative; no: stehen + dative
where (a state) / where to (a movement with a goal)
the Perfekt of stehen and stellen: both with haben, participle at the end

cards.title: Before we start: from „Wo ist das?“ to „Wohin stelle ich das?“
cards.body: The four of the WG have a free fifth room at the end of the Flur. Today only der Schrank and das Regal stand in it. Mira, Ben, Leon and Anna set it up, and later the WG looks for a new flatmate. To place things you need one test for the whole chapter: does somebody move the thing?
steps: You already know: two-way prepositions with Wo? and Wohin?, the verbs stehen and stellen in the present, and the Perfekt.
New today: ONE test for stehen or stellen (is there an object that somebody moves?), the Perfekt hat gestanden and hat gestellt, and ten words for furnishing a room.
By the end you can: say where a piece of furniture stands, say where you put it, and report both in the Perfekt.

examples.de: Das Sofa steht im Wohnzimmer.
examples.en: The sofa is in the living room.
examples.why: You know this already: steht = Wo? + dative.

examples.de: Ich gehe in die Küche.
examples.en: I go into the kitchen.
examples.why: You know this already: gehen = Wohin? + accusative.

examples.de: Ben stellt den Schrank in die Ecke.
examples.en: Ben puts the cupboard in the corner.
examples.why: New today: stellen has an object, so it goes Wohin?.

cards.more: Think of a moving day. Friends carry boxes and keep asking two things: Where is it? and Where do I put it? In English you already feel the difference, because 'is' and 'put' are two different words. German does the same with stehen and stellen. Today you get one test that sorts every sentence: is somebody moving the thing? If yes, ask Wohin?. If not, ask Wo?. After that, only the articles are left to choose.

cards.title: Two verbs, two questions
cards.body: Stehen says where a thing is: der Schrank steht in der Ecke. It has no object and answers Wo?, so it takes the dative. Stellen is an action: somebody puts a thing somewhere. It has an object and answers Wohin?, so it takes the accusative. The two verbs even sound alike, so look at the object.
cards.lead: You know that two-way prepositions can answer two questions. Here the verb itself decides, so this card sets the two verbs side by side with their question and their case.

examples.de: Der Schrank steht in der Ecke.
examples.en: The cupboard stands in the corner.

examples.de: Ben stellt den Schrank in die Ecke.
examples.en: Ben puts the cupboard in the corner.

examples.de: Die Lampe steht auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: The lamp is on the table.

deeper.text: Both verbs are regular in the present: er steht, er stellt. Stehen belongs to the thing: the cupboard stands there for days. Stellen belongs to a person: Ben does something. If you can ask „Who did it?“ and a person answers, take stellen. If nobody does anything, take stehen.

example.de: Der Hocker steht vor der Tür.
example.en: The stool stands in front of the door.

cards.more: English also has pairs: 'the cup is on the table' and 'I put the cup on the table'. German is just as tidy. Stehen is the quiet verb: the thing is there and nobody does anything. Stellen is the busy verb: a person holds the thing and moves it. Busy verb, busy question: Wohin? Quiet verb, quiet question: Wo? Try it with a cup near you: Die Tasse steht auf dem Tisch. Ich stelle die Tasse auf den Tisch.

rows: Der Schrank steht in der Ecke.
Ben stellt den Schrank in die Ecke.

steps: Ask: does somebody do something with the thing?
Yes, there is an object: stellen + accusative (Wohin?).
No, the thing just is there: stehen + dative (Wo?).

cards.title: The nine prepositions: a quick revision
cards.body: You know the nine two-way prepositions: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen. After Wo? the article is dative (dem, dem, der, den). After Wohin? it is accusative (den, das, die, die). Short forms: am, im, ans, ins, aufs. In the plural dative the noun ends in -n: neben den Kisten.
cards.lead: Before we use the test with all nine prepositions, here is the small grid you already know. Use it as a reference: the verb chooses the column, the gender chooses the article.

examples.de: Das Regal steht am Fenster.
examples.en: The shelf stands at the window.

examples.de: Ben stellt das Regal ans Fenster.
examples.en: Ben puts the shelf at the window.

examples.de: Die Lampe steht neben den Kisten.
examples.en: The lamp stands next to the boxes.

deeper.text: Only the nine prepositions switch between the two cases. All other prepositions you know stay fixed: mit is always dative, für is always accusative. For the nine the picture is the same every time: no movement means dative, a goal of a movement means accusative.

example.de: Leon stellt die Kommode hinter die Tür.
example.en: Leon puts the chest of drawers behind the door.

cards.more: Think of the grid as a vending machine with two buttons. Button one is the verb: a state gives you the dative column, a movement gives you the accusative column. Button two is the gender of the noun. Out comes the article. Practise with one noun of each gender and say the pairs aloud: dem Schrank, den Schrank. dem Regal, das Regal. der Kommode, die Kommode. In the plural, Kisten already ends in -n, so nothing is added.

cards.title: Furniture words: article and plural
cards.body: Learn every noun with its article and its plural, because the article decides the ending after Wo? and Wohin?. Say the whole chunk: der Hocker, die Hocker. Compound nouns take the article of the LAST part: Nacht + der Tisch = der Nachttisch; Bücher + das Regal = das Bücherregal.
cards.lead: You can now choose the verb and the case. This card gives you the furniture words you will move around in the free room, each with the article that makes the endings work.

examples.de: Die Steckdose ist hinter dem Regal.
examples.en: The socket is behind the shelf.

examples.de: Der Vorhang hängt am Fenster.
examples.en: The curtain hangs at the window.

examples.de: Ben stellt den Nachttisch neben das Bett.
examples.en: Ben puts the bedside table next to the bed.

deeper.text: Many plurals of furniture add an umlaut: der Schrank, die Schränke; der Vorhang, die Vorhänge. Words ending in -er or -el often stay the same: der Hocker, die Hocker; das Kabel, die Kabel. Words ending in -e add -n: die Kommode, die Kommoden. Learn the plural together with the singular, and you will rarely guess wrong.

example.de: Die Hocker stehen neben den Schränken.
example.en: The stools stand next to the cupboards.

cards.more: Treat every noun like a person with a name tag. The tag is the article: der, das or die. If you lose the tag, you cannot choose dem or den later. So never learn Hocker alone, always der Hocker. A second trick: the plural tells you the family. A word that ends in -e almost always takes -n, and a word that ends in -er or -el stays the same. Say each pair aloud once and you will remember it better than from a list.

cards.title: The object test with six pairs
cards.body: Here are three pairs of sentences. In each pair the thing and the place are the same: the left sentence is a state, the right one has a person who moves the thing. Look only at the verb and the object. No object means dative. An object that somebody moves means accusative. Here the preposition never tells you the case.
cards.lead: Now you try the test on real furniture. Read each row from left to right: same thing, same place, but a different verb and so a different case.

examples.de: Das Regal steht in der Ecke.
examples.en: The shelf stands in the corner.

examples.de: Anna stellt die Kommode ins Zimmer.
examples.en: Anna puts the chest of drawers into the room.

examples.de: Ben stellt die Hocker vor die Tür.
examples.en: Ben puts the stools in front of the door.

deeper.text: The object does not have to be a big piece of furniture. Small things work in the same way: Ich stelle die Tasse auf den Tisch. The cup is the object, the table is the goal. In the answer to Wohin? you often drop the object, but it is still there in your mind: Wohin? Auf den Tisch!

example.de: Ich stelle die Tasse auf den Tisch.
example.en: I put the cup on the table.

cards.more: A quick way to test yourself: cover one column with your hand. Read the left sentence and build the right one in your head, then swap. Notice what changes: the verb, the person who appears, the article. What stays the same: the thing, the place and the preposition. So the small word in or vor never decides the case. If you get stuck, ask: Does somebody do something to the thing? If yes, you need the accusative.

rows: Das Regal steht in der Ecke.
Leon stellt das Regal in die Ecke.
Anna stellt die Kommode ins Zimmer.
Die Hocker stehen vor der Tür.
Ben stellt die Hocker vor die Tür.

cards.title: The Perfekt: hat gestanden, hat gestellt, hat aufgestellt
cards.body: Both verbs take haben in the Perfekt. Stehen is irregular: hat gestanden. Stellen is regular: hat gestellt. Aufstellen (to set up) is separable, the ge sits in the middle: hat aufgestellt. As always the participle stands at the very END of the sentence, and the place phrase stays in the middle.
cards.lead: You already know the Perfekt bracket: haben in position 2, the participle at the end. Now you fill the bracket with the two new verbs and the separable aufstellen.

examples.de: Der Schrank hat in der Ecke gestanden.
examples.en: The cupboard stood in the corner.

examples.de: Ben hat den Schrank in die Ecke gestellt.
examples.en: Ben put the cupboard in the corner.

examples.de: Wir haben die Lampe aufgestellt.
examples.en: We set up the lamp.

deeper.text: In the south of Germany, in Austria and in Switzerland you also hear ist gestanden: Das Regal ist an der Wand gestanden. That is regional. In this course and in the north you always say hat gestanden. The meaning is the same, so you will understand both when you hear them.

example.de: Das Regal hat lange im Flur gestanden.
example.en: The shelf stood in the hallway for a long time.

cards.more: Compare with English: 'has stood' and 'has put'. English also keeps one participle for the end of the clause, and German does it even more strictly. Stehen is an old irregular verb, like English 'stand, stood', so its participle changes inside: gestanden. Stellen is regular, so it simply ends in -t: gestellt. A separable verb puts ge- in the middle: auf-ge-stellt. Say the three chunks aloud five times: hat gestanden, hat gestellt, hat aufgestellt.
steps: Haben in position 2.
The place phrase in the middle: in der Ecke / in die Ecke.
The participle at the very end: gestanden / gestellt / aufgestellt.

cards.title: Short answers, pronouns and the imperative
cards.body: Questions and answers are short. Wo? gets a state: Er steht am Fenster. Wohin? gets a command or a goal: Stell ihn ans Fenster! You know the accusative pronouns ihn (der), sie (die), es (das). The imperative du of stellen is Stell! without -st, and the preposition phrase stays after the object.
cards.lead: In real life you hardly ever repeat the whole sentence. This card shows how the room helpers ask and answer fast: question word, pronoun, and an imperative.

examples.de: Wo steht der Hocker?
examples.en: Where is the stool?

examples.de: Er steht am Fenster.
examples.en: It is at the window.

examples.de: Stell ihn ans Fenster!
examples.en: Put it at the window!

deeper.text: Wohin damit? is a chunk you know from the first course: it means „Where do I put this?“. The answer is usually an imperative with a pronoun: Stell es in die Ecke! Stell sie auf den Tisch! The pronoun replaces the object, so only the Wohin? phrase is left behind it.

example.de: Stell die Lampe auf den Schreibtisch!
example.en: Put the lamp on the desk!

cards.more: Picture a loud moving day: nobody has time for long sentences. Somebody shouts Wohin damit? and points. The helper answers with the shortest thing that works: Stell ihn ans Fenster! Three tiny tricks make this work. First, the pronoun copies the gender of the noun: der Hocker, so ihn. Second, the du-imperative of stellen has no -st: Stell! Third, the goal phrase keeps its accusative: ans Fenster, in die Ecke. Everything else is dropped because everybody can see it.

cards.title: In the free room: Ben and Anna set up
cards.body: Ben and Anna carry the first pieces into the free room. Read the dialogue and look for each sentence type: a question with Wohin?, an imperative with a pronoun, a state with stehen and a sentence with stellen and an object. One sentence also has a small adjective with its ending: die große Kommode, in die kleine Ecke.
cards.lead: Now everything comes together in one short scene. Read it twice: first for the meaning, then for the test question: who moves something?

examples.de: Ben: Wohin stellen wir das Bücherregal?
examples.en: Ben: Where do we put the bookshelf?

examples.de: Anna: Stell es an die Wand!
examples.en: Anna: Put it against the wall!

examples.de: Anna: Wir stellen die große Kommode in die kleine Ecke.
examples.en: Anna: We put the big chest of drawers in the small corner.
examples.why: Ending chip: after die the adjective ends in -e.

deeper.text: The dialogue shows a typical pattern: first Wohin? with stellen, then the answer in the imperative, then a state with stehen when the thing is already somewhere. Notice how the same chest of drawers appears in both forms: Die Kommode steht schon im Flur, then Ich stelle sie ins Zimmer.

example.de: Die Kommode steht schon im Flur.
example.en: The chest of drawers is already in the hallway.

cards.more: Treat the dialogue like a small treasure hunt. Read it once for the story. Then read it again with two coloured pens. Mark every verb that moves something (stellen, Stell!) in one colour, and every verb that only says where a thing is (steht) in the other. Next, underline each preposition phrase and check the article: after stellen it is accusative (an die Wand), after steht it is dative (im Flur). Finally, read it aloud with a friend, one role each.

rows: Dann stelle ich sie ins Zimmer.
Danke! Wir stellen die große Kommode in die kleine Ecke.

lessons.title: Das Bild hängt, ich hänge es auf: liegen, legen and hängen
lessons.goal: Use liegen and legen and the double verb hängen correctly, with the Perfekt, and hang and lay things in the room.

grammar.point: Liegen and legen work like stehen and stellen: no object means Wo? and the dative, an object that somebody moves means Wohin? and the accusative. Hängen is the same word in the present for both jobs. Perfekt: hat gelegen / hat gelegt, hat gehangen (it hangs) / hat gehängt (somebody hangs it); aufhängen is separable.
grammar.oneLine: Das Bild hängt an der Wand. Mira hängt das Bild an die Wand.

mistake.wrong: Ich hänge das Poster an der Wand auf.
mistake.right: Ich hänge das Poster an die Wand auf.
mistake.why: Hängen with an object (das Poster) answers Wohin?, so the preposition takes the accusative.

terms.meaning: to lie (a state, no object) / to lay something somewhere (with object)
the two Perfekt forms of hängen: it hangs / somebody hangs it
to hang up; separable: Mira hängt das Bild auf, hat aufgehängt

cards.title: Before we start: three pairs, one test
cards.body: The free room needs more than der Schrank. Mira wants der Teppich on the floor and das Poster over the bed. Leon looks for the hammer. Today the test from lesson 1 works for flat things (liegen and legen) and for things that hang. But hängen is special: it has two Perfekt forms.
steps: You already know: stehen and stellen, the object test (an object that somebody moves = Wohin? + accusative), and hat gestanden / hat gestellt.
New today: liegen and legen for flat things, hängen with and without an object, the Perfekt gehangen or gehängt, and the separable verb aufhängen.
By the end you can: say where a thing lies or hangs, say where you put it, and report both in the Perfekt.

examples.de: Der Schrank steht in der Ecke.
examples.en: The cupboard stands in the corner.
examples.why: You know this already: no object, Wo?, dative.

examples.de: Ben stellt ihn in die Ecke.
examples.en: Ben puts it in the corner.
examples.why: You know this already: an object, Wohin?, accusative.

examples.de: Leon legt den Teppich auf den Boden.
examples.en: Leon lays the carpet on the floor.
examples.why: New today: the same test with legen.

cards.more: Imagine a trip to the hardware store before the room is ready. You buy a hammer, nails, a ladder, a carpet. At home every item gets a job: some stand, some lie flat, some hang on the wall. German gives each job its own verb, and for every job you ask the two questions you already know: Wo? or Wohin? So today you add three verb pairs but no new rule. Only hängen is odd, because it has two Perfekt forms.

cards.title: liegen or legen: flat things
cards.body: Liegen says where a flat thing is: der Teppich liegt auf dem Boden. No object, so Wo? and the dative. Legen is the action: somebody puts a flat thing somewhere. Leon legt den Teppich auf den Boden. There is an object, so Wohin? and the accusative. It is exactly the same test as stehen and stellen.
cards.lead: In lesson 1 you separated stehen from stellen. Flat things work in the same way, so this card puts liegen and legen next to each other with the same question and case.

examples.de: Der Teppich liegt auf dem Boden.
examples.en: The carpet lies on the floor.

examples.de: Leon legt den Teppich auf den Boden.
examples.en: Leon lays the carpet on the floor.

examples.de: Das Handtuch liegt auf dem Bett.
examples.en: The towel lies on the bed.

deeper.text: Both verbs are regular in the present: er liegt, er legt. Only the Perfekt of liegen is special: hat gelegen. Watch out for the spelling: liegt (with ie) is the state, legt (with e) is the action. The vowel change from ie to e shows you the verb with the object.

example.de: Ich lege das Handtuch auf das Bett.
example.en: I put the towel on the bed.

cards.more: English has almost the same pair: 'to lie' and 'to lay'. The book lies on the table. I lay the book on the table. German keeps the two verbs clearly apart: liegen and legen. A hint for the spelling: liegen has the i, like 'lie', and legen has the e, like 'lay'. The verb with an object is the one with the e: legen. Say them as two little pictures: liegt means it rests, legt means somebody puts it.

rows: Der Teppich liegt auf dem Boden.
Leon legt den Teppich auf den Boden.

steps: Is the thing flat? Then use liegen or legen.
Does somebody move it (an object)? legen + accusative.
Does it just lie there? liegen + dative.

cards.title: hängen: one word, two jobs
cards.body: Hängen is the odd one: the present is the same for both jobs. Without an object it says where a thing is: das Bild hängt an der Wand (dative, Wo?). With an object it is an action: Mira hängt das Bild an die Wand (accusative, Wohin?). The word looks identical, so you must check the object again.
cards.lead: The first two pairs had two different verbs. Hängen has only one form in the present, so the object test is your only help here. This card shows both jobs.

examples.de: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
examples.en: The picture hangs on the wall.

examples.de: Mira hängt das Bild an die Wand.
examples.en: Mira hangs the picture on the wall.

examples.de: Die Lampe hängt über dem Tisch.
examples.en: The lamp hangs over the table.

deeper.text: English has the same trouble: „the picture hangs“ and „Mira hangs the picture“ use the same word. In German the object makes the difference in the case. If you can turn the sentence into „Somebody hangs it up“, there is an object and you take the accusative.

example.de: Leon hängt den Vorhang ans Fenster.
example.en: Leon hangs the curtain at the window.

cards.more: Look at the sentence like a photo with a person in it. Das Bild hängt: the photo shows only the picture on the wall. Mira hängt das Bild: the photo shows Mira with her arms up, holding the picture. A person doing something means an object in the sentence, and an object means accusative. English also uses one word for both: 'the coat hangs' and 'I hang the coat'. The question is the same as with stellen, only the verb never changes in the present.

rows: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
Mira hängt das Bild an die Wand.

steps: Is there an object that somebody moves?
Yes: hängen + accusative (Wohin?).
No: hängen + dative (Wo?).

cards.title: The Perfekt of all three pairs
cards.body: All six verbs use haben in the Perfekt. Stehen, liegen and the state-hängen are irregular and end in -en: gestanden, gelegen, gehangen. The action verbs stellen, legen and hängen are regular and end in -t: gestellt, gelegt, gehängt. Only hängen has the same infinitive for both: gehangen means it hangs, gehängt means somebody hangs it.
cards.lead: You know the Perfekt of stehen and stellen. Now the same pattern gets two more pairs, and hängen shows that the participle can even tell you which job the verb does.

examples.de: Das Poster hat zwei Wochen an der Wand gehangen.
examples.en: The poster hung on the wall for two weeks.

examples.de: Ich habe das Poster an die Wand gehängt.
examples.en: I hung the poster on the wall.

examples.de: Der Teppich hat auf dem Boden gelegen.
examples.en: The carpet lay on the floor.

deeper.text: There is a simple rule behind the forms: the verbs without an object keep their old irregular pattern (stehen, gestanden), the verbs with an object are regular (stellen, gestellt). Gelegen and gelegt look alike: gelegen has -en and belongs to liegen, gelegt has -t and belongs to legen.

example.de: Leon hat den Teppich auf den Boden gelegt.
example.en: Leon laid the carpet on the floor.

cards.more: Learn the Perfekt as a short rhyme in your head: quiet verbs wear -en, busy verbs wear -t. Gestanden, gelegen, gehangen: nobody moves. Gestellt, gelegt, gehängt: somebody moves a thing. The vowel also shows it: gehangen has a, gehängt has ä. When you write the Perfekt, ask first: object or no object? The ending follows. And never mix up gelegen and gelegt: one letter, a different job.

cards.title: Separable: aufhängen, aufstellen, hinlegen
cards.body: Aufhängen (to hang up) is separable like aufstellen. In the present the small part goes to the end: Mira hängt das Bild auf. The goal stays in the middle: Mira hängt das Bild an die Wand auf. In the Perfekt the ge sits in the middle: sie hat das Bild aufgehängt. Hinlegen works in the same way.
cards.lead: You know separable verbs from the earlier chapters. This card shows how they work with a Wohin? phrase: the goal stands in the middle and the small part waits at the end.

examples.de: Mira hängt das Bild auf.
examples.en: Mira hangs up the picture.

examples.de: Mira hängt das Bild an die Wand auf.
examples.en: Mira hangs the picture on the wall.
examples.why: The goal stays in the middle.

examples.de: Sie hat das Bild aufgehängt.
examples.en: She has hung up the picture.

deeper.text: Aufhängen and aufstellen always need an object: somebody hangs or sets up something, so the goal is accusative. Hinlegen works the same with a thing (Leon legt den Hammer hin). With a person it becomes reflexive: Ich lege mich hin, as in chapter 4. You can order all of them too: Häng das Poster bitte auf!

example.de: Leon legt den Hammer hin.
example.en: Leon puts the hammer down.

cards.more: Think of a sandwich. The top bread is hängt, the bottom bread is auf, and the goal an die Wand is the filling in the middle. That is the present: Mira hängt das Bild an die Wand auf. In the Perfekt the bread closes into one word, aufgehängt, and the filling sits between hat and the participle. English works in a similar way: 'hang the picture up'. The small part moves away from its verb, and German sends it to the end.

cards.title: The tool box: words for hanging things
cards.body: Hanging a poster needs tools. Learn each word with its article and plural: der Hammer, der Nagel, die Schraube, die Bohrmaschine. Das Werkzeug means tools in general. The ladder is die Leiter. Verb + noun makes a mini-sentence: Der Hammer liegt, die Leiter steht, das Poster hängt.
cards.lead: You can now place things with six verbs. This card gives you the small words around the job: tools and things to hang, each with article and plural, ready for the drills.

examples.de: Leon holt die Bohrmaschine und die Schrauben.
examples.en: Leon gets the drill and the screws.

examples.de: Das Werkzeug liegt im Flur.
examples.en: The tools are in the hallway.

examples.de: Mira stellt die Leiter neben den Schrank.
examples.en: Mira puts the ladder next to the cupboard.

deeper.text: German builds many words from two parts, and the last part gives the article: das Werkzeug = Werk (work) + Zeug (stuff); das Handtuch = Hand + Tuch (cloth); die Bohrmaschine = bohren (to drill) + die Maschine. When you meet a long new word, split it: the meaning and the gender both appear.

example.de: Das Handtuch liegt auf dem Bett.
example.en: The towel lies on the bed.

cards.more: A tool box is a good place to learn word families. Open it in your head: Werkzeug is the big word, the box itself. Inside you find der Hammer, der Nagel, die Schraube. Say each word with its article, then tie it to a verb: der Hammer liegt, die Leiter steht, das Poster hängt. A noun plus a verb makes a mini-sentence that is easy to remember. After a week you will say it without thinking.

cards.title: Sort the room: standing, lying, hanging
cards.body: A rule of thumb for the room. Things that stand upright stehen. Flat things on a surface liegen. Things that are fixed to a wall or hang from above hängen. Choose the verb by the shape of the thing, then choose the case by the object test. The kind of thing and the verb go together almost every time.
cards.lead: Now you look at the whole room. The sorting table shows seven things and the verb that belongs to each one, so you can pick the right verb without thinking.

examples.de: Die Kiste steht auf dem Boden.
examples.en: The box is on the floor.

examples.de: Das Kissen liegt auf dem Sofa.
examples.en: The cushion lies on the sofa.

examples.de: Die Gardine hängt am Fenster.
examples.en: The net curtain hangs at the window.

deeper.text: The rule is a help, not a law. A towel can lie on the bed (flat) or hang on the door (from above). A book can stand in the shelf (upright) or lie on the table (flat). So look at the real picture: how is the thing placed right now? Then the verb follows.

example.de: Das Handtuch hängt an der Tür.
example.en: The towel hangs on the door.

cards.more: Imagine you walk through the room with a camera and name what you see. The wardrobe stands, the rug lies, the curtain hangs. Do it every day for a week with things in your own flat: Die Tasse steht. Das Handy liegt. Die Jacke hängt. It takes two minutes and the verbs stick fast. If a thing can be placed in two ways, like a towel, the verb tells the picture: Das Handtuch liegt (flat) or Das Handtuch hängt (from a hook).

cards.title: With tools: Mira and Leon hang the poster
cards.body: Mira and Leon hang the first poster in the free room. Read the dialogue and look for the verbs: liegt describes where the Hammer is, hängen asks for the goal and the imperative gives the answer. At the end the state-hängt appears, and the picture is finished. Notice that ich hole die Leiter has no position verb.
cards.lead: The last card puts everything together in a short scene. First find the verbs in the dialogue, then check with the object test whether each case is right.

examples.de: Mira: Hast du den Hammer?
examples.en: Mira: Have you got the hammer?

examples.de: Leon: Er liegt auf dem Boden.
examples.en: Leon: It is lying on the floor.

examples.de: Leon: Häng es über das Bett!
examples.en: Leon: Hang it over the bed!

deeper.text: See how the dialogue switches between the two pictures. Wohin hängen wir das Poster? asks for the goal, so the answer is an imperative and the accusative: über das Bett. A moment later the poster is up, and the same words give the state: Jetzt hängt es über dem Bett.

example.de: Jetzt hängt es über dem Bett.
example.en: Now it is hanging over the bed.

cards.more: Read the dialogue aloud and act it out. When Leon says Er liegt auf dem Boden, point at the floor: a state, the hammer just lies there. When he says Häng es über das Bett, point up and move your hand: a movement with a goal. Your hands show you the case. Hand still: dative. Hand moving: accusative. The more you connect the verbs with gestures, the less you have to think about the rule.

rows: Gut. Ich lege die Nägel aufs Bett.
Danke! Jetzt hängt es über dem Bett.

lessons.title: Ich setze mich aufs Sofa: sitzen, setzen and sich setzen
lessons.goal: Use sitzen and sich setzen, sich legen and sich stellen with two-way phrases, and add movement verbs with a goal and a result.

grammar.topic: sitzen / sich setzen and movement verbs
grammar.point: A person puts himself somewhere with a reflexive verb: sich setzen, sich legen, sich stellen + accusative (Wohin?). The state uses sitzen, liegen, stehen + dative (Wo?). Perfekt: hat gesessen, hat sich gesetzt, hat sich gelegt, hat sich gestellt. Movement verbs (springen, klettern, rennen) take the accusative for the goal and sein in the Perfekt; the result is a state with the dative.
grammar.oneLine: Anna sitzt auf dem Sofa. Anna setzt sich auf das Sofa.

mistake.wrong: Ich sitze mich auf das Sofa.
mistake.right: Ich setze mich auf das Sofa.
mistake.why: Sitzen has no object. For moving yourself to a seat use setzen with mich: it answers Wohin? with the accusative.

terms.meaning: to sit down (action, reflexive pronoun, accusative) / to be sitting (state, dative)
to lie down, to go and stand somewhere: the same test as sich setzen
Perfekt of a movement verb: sein, participle at the end; the result is a state with the dative

cards.title: Before we start: people and animals move themselves
cards.body: The free room is almost ready, and now the people use it. Anna tries der Hocker, Ben prefers der Boden, and the Katze of Frau Weber visits from the Treppenhaus. People and animals can put themselves somewhere: sich setzen, sich legen, sich stellen. The test stays the same.
steps: You already know: sich setzen and sich hinlegen as reflexive verbs, and the pairs stehen / stellen and liegen / legen.
New today: sitzen and sich setzen with a place, the same for sich legen and sich stellen, the Perfekt, and movement verbs like springen with a goal.
By the end you can: say where somebody sits, where he sits down, and where an animal jumps.

examples.de: Ich setze mich.
examples.en: I sit down.
examples.why: You know this already: sich setzen.

examples.de: Ich habe mich hingelegt.
examples.en: I lay down.
examples.why: You know this already: sich hinlegen in the Perfekt.

examples.de: Anna setzt sich auf das Sofa.
examples.en: Anna sits down on the sofa.
examples.why: New today: a place with the accusative.

cards.more: Think about a café. You walk in, look around and sit down: first you go to the table, then you sit. German has one verb for the going-to-sit and another for the sitting. When you add mich, dich or sich, you are the thing that moves, so the place after it answers Wohin? and takes the accusative. Today you meet three of these verbs and a new group: verbs of real movement, like jumping and climbing.

cards.title: sitzen or sich setzen
cards.body: Sitzen says where somebody is: Anna sitzt auf dem Sofa. No object, so Wo? and the dative. Sich setzen is the action of sitting down: Anna setzt sich auf das Sofa. The reflexive pronoun sich is the object, so Wohin? and the accusative follow. The pronoun mich, dich or sich is a part of the verb.
cards.lead: People can be the thing that moves. The pronoun sich stands for the person who moves, so it works as the object in your test. This card compares the state and the action.

examples.de: Anna sitzt auf dem Sofa.
examples.en: Anna is sitting on the sofa.

examples.de: Anna setzt sich auf das Sofa.
examples.en: Anna sits down on the sofa.

examples.de: Mira sitzt am Tisch.
examples.en: Mira is sitting at the table.

deeper.text: English often uses one phrase for both ideas, German keeps them apart. Sitzen is like a photo: she is sitting. Sich setzen is like a short film: she goes from standing to sitting. In the short film something moves, and the person herself is the thing that moves.

example.de: Mira setzt sich an den Tisch.
example.en: Mira sits down at the table.

cards.more: Learn sich setzen as one block, like a train with a pronoun at its back. Ich setze mich. Du setzt dich. Er setzt sich. The pronoun is not decoration: without it you only say where somebody is. Compare: Ich sitze auf dem Sofa (I am there already) and Ich setze mich auf das Sofa (I am going there to sit). English hides the same difference in one word, 'sit', and you only know it from the context. German shows it in the verb.

rows: Mira setzt sich an den Tisch.

steps: Does the person only stay where she is? sitzen + dative.
Does she move to a new place? sich setzen + accusative.
Put the reflexive pronoun right after the verb.

cards.title: Three reflexive pairs
cards.body: The same idea works for lying and standing. Liegen and stehen describe a state, sich legen and sich stellen describe how a person gets there. The reflexive pronoun is the object, so the place that follows is Wohin? and accusative. Three pairs: sitzen and sich setzen, liegen and sich legen, stehen and sich stellen.
cards.lead: You know that people can put themselves somewhere. Here are all three pairs in one table, so you can see that the reflexive pronoun is the only new piece.

examples.de: Ich setze mich auf den Hocker.
examples.en: I sit down on the stool.

examples.de: Ben legt sich aufs Bett.
examples.en: Ben lies down on the bed.

examples.de: Leon stellt sich ans Fenster.
examples.en: Leon steps up to the window.

deeper.text: Sich stellen has a special meaning with people: you take a position, you stand up somewhere. Leon stellt sich ans Fenster means that he goes and stands there. You hear it for a person who walks over to a place and stops: Stell dich neben mich!

example.de: Stell dich neben mich!
example.en: Stand next to me!

cards.more: Think of a game with a small child: 'Sit! Lie! Stand!' You use the state words when the child is already there, and the action words when you place the child somewhere. For yourself it is the same, only now you are the child. Ich sitze: I am there already. Ich setze mich: I move myself there. Do the same with liegen and stehen. The pronoun mich is the whole difference, plus the case of the place that follows.

rows: Ich setze mich auf den Hocker.

cards.title: The Perfekt: hat gesessen, hat sich gesetzt
cards.body: In the Perfekt, sitzen, liegen and stehen use haben: hat gesessen, hat gelegen, hat gestanden. The reflexive verbs also use haben, with the reflexive pronoun right after it: hat sich gesetzt, hat sich gelegt, hat sich gestellt. The participle stands at the very end of the sentence.
cards.lead: You know the Perfekt bracket with haben and the participle. Now the reflexive pronoun fits in directly after haben, and the participle still waits at the end.

examples.de: Anna hat lange auf dem Sofa gesessen.
examples.en: Anna sat on the sofa for a long time.

examples.de: Anna hat sich auf das Sofa gesetzt.
examples.en: Anna sat down on the sofa.

examples.de: Ben hat sich aufs Bett gelegt.
examples.en: Ben lay down on the bed.

deeper.text: You can see the two pictures in the Perfekt too. Hat gesessen is a long time (lange auf dem Sofa gesessen), hat sich gesetzt is one moment (she sat down). Do not use sein with them: sitzen and the three reflexive verbs always take haben in this course.

example.de: Leon hat sich ans Fenster gestellt.
example.en: Leon stepped up to the window.

cards.more: Count the order on your fingers: Anna (1) hat (2) sich (3) auf das Sofa (4) gesetzt (5). The pronoun sits right behind the helper verb, and the participle waits at the end. English says 'Anna sat down' and puts the 'down' last. German pays with one extra word, sich, but the order is easy to learn. Say this one sentence ten times, then swap the place: aufs Bett, ans Fenster, auf den Hocker.
steps: Haben in position 2.
The reflexive pronoun right after it: sich, mich, dich.
The place phrase, then the participle at the very end.

cards.title: Movement verbs: springen, klettern, rennen
cards.body: The verbs springen, klettern and rennen move a person or an animal to a goal. The goal answers Wohin? and takes the accusative: die Katze springt auf den Tisch. In the Perfekt they use sein: ist gesprungen, ist geklettert, ist gerannt. The result is a state with the dative: jetzt sitzt sie auf dem Tisch.
cards.lead: You know that gehen and fahren take the accusative for a goal. These three movement verbs do the same, and they show the whole story: the movement and then the result.

examples.de: Die Katze springt auf den Tisch.
examples.en: The cat jumps onto the table.

examples.de: Ben klettert auf die Leiter.
examples.en: Ben climbs onto the ladder.

examples.de: Leon rennt in die Küche.
examples.en: Leon runs into the kitchen.

deeper.text: In the Perfekt the verb changes its helper: sein, because the person or the animal gets to a new place. Die Katze ist auf den Tisch gesprungen. A moment later the picture changes to a state: Jetzt sitzt sie auf dem Tisch. The movement has the accusative, the new place has the dative.

example.de: Die Katze ist auf den Tisch gesprungen.
example.en: The cat has jumped onto the table.

cards.more: Think of a film with two scenes. Scene one: the cat springt. It is on its way, so the goal gets Wohin? and the accusative, and the Perfekt uses sein because the cat changes its place. Scene two: the cat sitzt on the table, and the state gets Wo? and the dative. A wrong sentence mixes the scenes: Die Katze sitzt auf den Tisch is wrong, because sitting is a state and not a goal. Tell the cat's story in two steps: ist gesprungen, then sitzt.

rows: Die Katze springt auf den Tisch.

cards.title: Seats and the stairwell: new words
cards.body: Seats: der Sitzsack, der Liegestuhl, der Gartenstuhl, die Hängematte. The house: das Treppenhaus, die Stufe, das Geländer, das Fensterbrett, das Dach. Learn each with its article and plural, then tie it to a verb: Der Sitzsack liegt, die Hängematte hängt, der Gartenstuhl steht.
cards.lead: You can now say who sits, lies or stands where. This card adds the words for the places and seats around the free room and the stairwell, so your sentences have something to talk about.

examples.de: Die Katze sitzt auf dem Fensterbrett.
examples.en: The cat is sitting on the windowsill.

examples.de: Anna setzt sich auf den Sitzsack.
examples.en: Anna sits down on the beanbag.

examples.de: Ben steht am Geländer.
examples.en: Ben is standing at the banister.

deeper.text: Many German seats are compounds that tell you their job: der Liegestuhl is a chair to lie in (liegen), der Sitzsack is a sack to sit in (sitzen), der Gartenstuhl is a chair for the garden. The first part is often a verb stem. When you know the verb, you can often guess the noun.

example.de: Der Liegestuhl steht im Garten.
example.en: The deck chair is in the garden.

cards.more: Try a sticky-note game. Take five pieces of paper and write one word on each: die Stufe, das Fensterbrett, das Geländer, das Dach, der Sitzsack. Put each paper next to the thing in your home, or next to a picture of it. Then say a sentence with a verb from this lesson: Ich setze mich auf die Stufe. Der Sitzsack liegt am Fenster. The notes give you the article, and the sentence gives you the case.

cards.title: Wo? Wohin? Woher?: questions with people and places
cards.body: Three question words for places. Wo? asks where somebody is: dative. Wohin? asks where somebody goes: accusative. Woher? asks where from: aus or von with the dative. Short forms are common in answers: aufs Sofa, am Tisch, ans Fenster.
cards.lead: This card is a revision of three question words from the earlier chapters. Here they appear together with the verbs of this lesson, so you can ask about every situation in the room.

examples.de: Wo sitzt Anna?
examples.en: Where is Anna sitting?

examples.de: Wohin setzt sie sich?
examples.en: Where does she sit down?

examples.de: Die Katze kommt aus dem Treppenhaus.
examples.en: The cat comes from the stairwell.

deeper.text: Woher? is the same question as „from where?“. The answer begins with aus (out of a room or a house) or with von (from a person or a point), always with the dative. For the cat the stairwell is a place she was in, so you say aus dem Treppenhaus. Short answers need no verb: Aus dem Treppenhaus.

example.de: Auf dem Sofa.
example.en: On the sofa.

cards.more: Ask the question first, and the answer picks its own case. Wo? is a place to be: dative. Wohin? is a goal: accusative. Woher? is a place you left: aus or von with the dative. A good drill: stand in the middle of your room, look at one object and ask all three questions about it. Wo ist die Lampe? Wohin stelle ich sie? Woher kommt sie? Three questions, three answers, and the question word chooses for you.

cards.title: In the free room: Anna, Ben and Mira
cards.body: The three of them try the free room. Read the dialogue and find three kinds of sentences: the imperative with a reflexive pronoun (Setz dich! Leg dich!), the state with sitzen and bleiben, and the action with sich setzen. For guests there is a polite version: Setzen Sie sich bitte! or Nehmen Sie Platz!
cards.lead: The last card of the lesson shows the three verbs in one conversation. Read the dialogue and check each sentence with the object test.

examples.de: Anna: Setz dich auf den Hocker!
examples.en: Anna: Sit down on the stool!

examples.de: Ben: Ich sitze lieber auf dem Boden.
examples.en: Ben: I prefer to sit on the floor.

examples.de: Mira: Dann leg dich auf das Bett!
examples.en: Mira: Then lie down on the bed!

deeper.text: The imperative of a reflexive verb is short: the verb first, then the pronoun dich: Setz dich! Leg dich! For the polite Sie form the pronoun is sich: Setzen Sie sich bitte! You hear it with guests and strangers, for example when Herr Ali welcomes guests in the restaurant „Zum Löwen“. Nehmen Sie Platz! is a polite invitation: take a seat.

example.de: Setzen Sie sich bitte!
example.en: Please sit down!

cards.more: Notice how Ben says no. He does not repeat the imperative. He answers with a state: Ich sitze lieber auf dem Boden. He is already on the floor, so nothing moves: Wo? and the dative. The others ask him to move somewhere new with imperatives, and those take the accusative. A real conversation always mixes both pictures. When you read, ask one small question about each line: does somebody get a new place? If yes, accusative. If not, dative.

lessons.title: Kannst du mir helfen? Ask for a favour
lessons.goal: Ask a friend or a neighbour for a favour with Kannst du, Könntest du or Könnten Sie and a Wohin? phrase, give short moving-day instructions and accept or refuse politely.

grammar.topic: Requests: können/könnte + infinitive at the end, or the imperative
grammar.point: Ask in three strengths: the imperative (Stell den Karton bitte in den Flur!), Kannst du … (normal) or Könntest du / Könnten Sie … (very polite). With a modal the infinitive goes to the END and the Wohin? phrase (accusative) sits in the middle. Separable verbs in the imperative send the prefix to the end: Pack die Kisten ein!

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Stell ihn ans Fenster!' to 'Könntest du ihn bitte ans Fenster stellen?'
cards.body: Mira has a heavy Schrank for the free room, and she cannot carry it alone. She needs help from her flatmates and from the neighbours. In lesson 1 you gave short orders with Wohin? phrases. Today you turn them into friendly requests, and you learn to say yes or no politely.
steps: You already know: the imperative (Stell die Lampe auf den Tisch!), Wohin? + accusative, and Könnten Sie mir helfen? from A2 chapter 5.
New today: three ways to ask for the same thing, each with a place phrase, polite answers, and the chunk Ich habe eine Bitte.
By the end you can: ask a friend or a neighbour for help with a move, give short instructions, and accept or refuse with a reason.

examples.de: Stell die Lampe bitte auf den Tisch!
examples.en: Please put the lamp on the table!
examples.why: You know this already: a direct imperative.

examples.de: Könntest du die Lampe bitte auf den Tisch stellen?

examples.why: New today: the same wish, very politely.

examples.de: Ich habe eine Bitte.
examples.en: I have a request.
examples.why: New today: a friendly way to start.

cards.more: Imagine the same wish in three voices. A friend yells: Stell den Karton in den Flur! A flatmate asks: Kannst du den Karton in den Flur stellen? A neighbour hears: Könnten Sie den Karton bitte in den Flur stellen? The box goes to the same place, but the voices sound different. In German, politeness lives mostly in the verb form and in the little words bitte and leider. Today you learn to pick the right voice for the right person, and then to say yes or no kindly.

cards.title: Ask for help: friend or neighbour
cards.body: Three easy openers: Kannst du mir helfen? Hast du kurz Zeit? Ich habe eine Bitte. To a neighbour or to Herr Ali you use Sie: Können Sie mir helfen? Haben Sie kurz Zeit? Typical answers: Klar! Gern! Or: Tut mir leid, ich habe keine Zeit.
cards.lead: The intro showed why Mira needs help. This card gives you the first sentence you say: three openers for a friend with du, the same for a neighbour with Sie, and the short answers.

examples.de: Kannst du mir helfen?
examples.en: Can you help me?

examples.de: Haben Sie kurz Zeit?
examples.en: Do you have a moment?

examples.de: Ich habe eine Bitte.
examples.en: I have a request.

examples.de: Tut mir leid, ich habe keine Zeit.
examples.en: Sorry, I have no time.

deeper.text: Ich habe eine Bitte works with du and with Sie, because it is about you, not about the other person. It is a soft start: the other person knows a question is coming and can listen. After it, you ask the real question. The noun is die Bitte, plural die Bitten, and it never changes with the person you talk to.

example.de: Frau Weber, ich habe eine Bitte. Haben Sie kurz Zeit?
example.en: Frau Weber, I have a request. Do you have a moment?

cards.more: Before the real question, people often knock on the door first. Hast du kurz Zeit? is a knock. Ich habe eine Bitte is a knock too. The other person gets two seconds to get ready and says Klar or Was gibt's? (what's up?). Only then comes your real question. English does this as well: 'Have you got a minute?' or 'Can I ask you something?' So the habit is not new. You only have to use du with friends and Sie with neighbours and Herr Ali.

rows: Tut mir leid, ich habe keine Zeit.

cards.title: Three ways to ask, one wish
cards.body: You can ask for the same thing in three ways. The imperative is direct: Stell den Karton bitte in den Flur! Kannst du … is normal. Könntest du … is very polite. With kannst and könntest the infinitive stellen goes to the END, and the Wohin? phrase sits in the middle.
cards.lead: Now you can open the conversation. This card shows the real question in three strengths, from direct to very polite, and where the second verb goes.

examples.de: Stell den Karton bitte in den Flur!
examples.en: Put the box in the hall, please!

examples.de: Kannst du den Karton bitte in den Flur stellen?
examples.en: Can you put the box in the hall, please?

examples.de: Könntest du den Karton bitte in den Flur stellen?
examples.en: Could you put the box in the hall, please?

deeper.text: Why accusative in den Flur? Because stellen has an object that moves: the Karton goes somewhere, so you ask Wohin? This does not change when you make the sentence polite. The bracket only moves stellen to the end. The same works with legen and hängen: Könntest du das Bild an die Wand hängen? The place phrase stays accusative.

example.de: Könntest du das Bild an die Wand hängen?
example.en: Could you hang the picture on the wall?

cards.more: Imagine a little bridge. On the left end stands kannst or könntest, on the right end stands the infinitive. Everything you want to say walks across the bridge: du, den Karton, bitte, in den Flur. The bridge only works if both ends are there. English has a similar bridge: 'Could you put the box in the hall?' But there, put stays next to could. In German the second verb runs all the way to the end, so the listener waits for it until the last word.
steps: Imperative = direct: Stell den Karton bitte in den Flur!
Kannst du … = normal: modal in position 2
Könntest du … = very polite: same order
The Wohin? phrase in the middle: in den Flur
The infinitive at the END: stellen

cards.title: Könnten Sie bitte …? to a neighbour
cards.body: To a neighbour you say Könnten Sie bitte …? Only könnten, nothing else. Könnten Sie mir bitte beim Tragen helfen? (beim = bei dem). The Sie imperative is also fine: Stellen Sie das Fahrrad bitte in den Keller. Good answers: Natürlich! or Gern, wohin soll ich es stellen?
cards.lead: You asked a friend with könntest. Now Mira asks neighbours, so she needs Sie: könnten Sie, the polite Sie imperative, and the answers a neighbour gives back.

examples.de: Könnten Sie mir bitte beim Tragen helfen?
examples.en: Could you help me carry, please?

examples.de: Stellen Sie das Fahrrad bitte in den Keller.
examples.en: Please put the bike in the cellar.

examples.de: Gern, wohin soll ich es stellen?
examples.en: Sure, where should I put it?

deeper.text: Beim Tragen means while carrying. Beim is bei dem, and the verb tragen becomes a noun with a capital letter: das Tragen. You can do this with many verbs: beim Einpacken, beim Aufbauen. For now, use it only after helfen: Könnten Sie mir beim Einpacken helfen? It sounds natural and very friendly.

example.de: Könnten Sie mir beim Einpacken helfen?
example.en: Could you help me with the packing?

cards.more: Think of the Sie-form as a polite hat that you put on your request. With Sie you never use kannst or könntest, because those belong to du. You use können or könnten, and Sie comes right after it. Then the sentence works as before: the infinitive goes to the end. Neighbours often say yes and ask back: Wohin soll ich es stellen? That is a good sign, because now you only have to point and say: In den Keller, bitte.

Natürlich! / Gern, wohin soll ich es stellen?

cards.title: Instructions for the Umzug
cards.body: In Germany many people build their furniture themselves. On moving day friends help, and later everyone eats pizza together. The instructions are short imperatives, often with separable verbs: the prefix goes to the end. Pack die Kisten ein! Räum die Regale ein! Trag den Tisch ins Zimmer!
cards.lead: You know how to ask politely. On moving day there is no time for long questions, so this card gives the short instructions: du imperatives with separable verbs and Wohin? phrases.

examples.de: Pack die Kisten ein!
examples.en: Pack the boxes!

examples.de: Trag den Tisch ins Zimmer!
examples.en: Carry the table into the room!

examples.de: Räum die Regale ein!
examples.en: Fill the shelves!

examples.de: Verschieb den Schrank bitte ein Stück nach links.
examples.en: Please move the wardrobe a bit to the left.

deeper.text: With ihr, for two or more friends, the imperative ends in -t: Packt die Kisten ein! Helft mit! With mithelfen the vowel changes only for du: Hilf mit! The prefix still goes to the end. Verschieben is not separable: ver- always stays on the verb, so you say Verschieb den Schrank!

example.de: Leon, Ben, helft bitte mit!
example.en: Leon, Ben, please help out!

cards.more: Imagine a relay race with moving boxes. Each helper gets one very short order: Pack ein! Trag das! Räum aus! The verb stands first, and if it has a front part like ein, aus or mit, that part runs to the end of the sentence. Notice that you never say du or ihr: the verb ending already shows who you mean. With a group of friends use the ihr-form, which ends in -t: Packt die Kisten ein! Helft mit!

cards.title: Moving-day words
cards.body: Nouns: die Bitte, die Hilfe, der Helfer, die Helferin, der Umzugswagen. Verbs with a front part: einpacken, auspacken, einräumen, ausräumen, mithelfen. Verschieben has no separable part. Learn the verbs as du-orders: Pack ein! Pack aus! Räum ein! Räum aus! Hilf mit! The front part always ends up last.
cards.lead: You can ask, instruct and answer. This card collects the words you will say again and again on moving day, so the next questions only test what you have already learned.

examples.de: Brauchst du Hilfe?
examples.en: Do you need help?

examples.de: Der Umzugswagen steht vor dem Haus.
examples.en: The removal van is in front of the house.

examples.de: Alle haben mitgeholfen.
examples.en: Everybody helped out.

deeper.text: Add -in to name a woman: der Helfer, die Helferin; der Nachbar, die Nachbarin. The plural of -in words is -innen: die Helferinnen. Words for men in -er keep the same plural: die Helfer. Die Hilfe is uncountable and has no plural: you say viel Hilfe or keine Hilfe, never Hilfen.

example.de: Eine Helferin trägt die Kisten.
example.en: A helper carries the boxes.

cards.more: Moving words come in pairs of opposites: einpacken and auspacken, einräumen and ausräumen. Ein- means into, aus- means out. Picture a box: you pack things into it, and later you take them out. The same with a wardrobe: you räumen things in or out. So when you know ein and aus, you learn two verbs for the price of one. Say the pairs aloud: ein, aus, ein, aus.

cards.title: Say yes or no politely
cards.body: If you can help: Gern! or Gern, aber nur eine Stunde. If you cannot, give a reason with denn or deshalb: Ich kann leider nicht, denn ich muss arbeiten. Ich habe keine Zeit. Deshalb kann ich nicht helfen. Then thanks: Danke, das ist nett! Kein Problem!
cards.lead: Someone has asked you for help. This card is about your answer: a warm yes, a yes with a limit, or a no with a reason, and then the thank-you.

examples.de: Gern, aber nur eine Stunde.
examples.en: Sure, but only for an hour.

examples.de: Ich kann leider nicht, denn ich muss arbeiten.
examples.en: Unfortunately I can't, because I have to work.

examples.de: Ich habe keine Zeit. Deshalb kann ich nicht helfen.
examples.en: I have no time. So I can't help.

examples.de: Danke, das ist nett!
examples.en: Thanks, that's kind!

deeper.text: Leider makes a no softer: Ich kann leider nicht. You can also offer another time, so the no is only half a no: Heute kann ich leider nicht, aber am Samstag habe ich Zeit. The person can plan again. To thank a friend you can also say Das ist nett von dir. To a neighbour: Das ist nett von Ihnen.

example.de: Heute kann ich leider nicht, aber am Samstag habe ich Zeit.
example.en: Unfortunately I can't today, but I have time on Saturday.

cards.more: A no is perfectly fine in Germany, and people like it when you are clear. Make it soft with three small tricks: say leider, give a short reason, and offer another day. Ich kann leider nicht, denn ich muss arbeiten. Aber am Sonntag habe ich Zeit. Then nobody is offended. And if you say yes, say Gern! with a smile. Whoever helps gets a Danke, das ist nett! Practise one yes and one no with a friend, out loud.

cards.title: Mini dialogue: Mira asks Leon
cards.body: Read the dialogue. Mira opens with Ich habe eine Bitte, then asks with Könntest du. Leon says yes and asks Wohin? Mira gives an instruction. At the end Leon reports in the Perfekt: Ich habe den Schrank an die Wand gestellt. Mira thanks him.
cards.lead: You now have every piece: the opener, the polite question, the instruction and the answer. On this card they come together in one short conversation about the Schrank.

examples.de: Leon, ich habe eine Bitte. Könntest du mir beim Umzug helfen?

examples.de: Gern. Wohin soll ich den Schrank stellen?
examples.en: Sure. Where should I put the wardrobe?

examples.de: Verschieb ihn bitte ein Stück nach links.
examples.en: Please move it a bit to the left.

examples.de: Ich habe den Schrank an die Wand gestellt.
examples.en: I have put the wardrobe against the wall.

examples.de: Danke, das ist nett!
examples.en: Thanks, that's kind!

deeper.text: Look at the last line by Leon. Gestellt is the Perfekt of stellen, and the place phrase is still accusative: an die Wand. The Perfekt does not change the case. The Schrank moved, so it is Wohin? Now it stands there: Der Schrank steht an der Wand. That is Wo? with the dative.

example.de: Jetzt steht der Schrank an der Wand.
example.en: Now the wardrobe is standing against the wall.

cards.more: Read the dialogue like a small play. First Mira asks nicely, then Leon says yes and asks where the box goes, Mira points, Leon pushes it and reports what he did. Mira says thanks. Read it twice, once as Mira and once as Leon. The second time, change the thing: not Schrank, but Regal or Fahrrad. Wohin soll ich es stellen? works for every thing, and only the article changes: den Schrank becomes das Regal.

Ask: Könntest du mir beim Umzug helfen?
Answer and ask back: Gern. Wohin soll ich …?
Instruct: Verschieb ihn bitte …
Report in the Perfekt: Ich habe … gestellt.
Thank: Danke, das ist nett!

lessons.title: Es stört mich, dass …: complain politely
lessons.goal: Complain politely about noise, rubbish and shoes in the Hausflur with Es stört mich, dass …, ask for a change, and react well to a complaint.

grammar.topic: dass-clauses in complaints: with a Wo? phrase and with the Perfekt
grammar.point: After Es stört mich / Ich finde es nicht gut / Ich ärgere mich comes a comma and a dass-clause with the verb at the END. If something just stands or lies there, use a Wo? phrase (dative) + stehen/liegen: …, dass die Schuhe im Hausflur stehen. If someone put it there, use the Perfekt with a Wohin? phrase (accusative), participle then haben last: …, dass Sie die Kiste in den Hausflur gestellt haben.
grammar.oneLine: Es stört mich, dass die Schuhe im Hausflur stehen.

mistake.wrong: Es stört mich, dass die Schuhe stehen im Hausflur.
mistake.right: Es stört mich, dass die Schuhe im Hausflur stehen.
mistake.why: In a dass-clause the verb goes to the very end, after the place phrase.

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich finde es gut, dass …' to 'Es stört mich, dass …'
cards.body: Living together is not always easy. Shoes stand in the Hausflur, the Müll is in front of the door, and Ben's music was loud last night. Frau Weber is not happy. In A2 chapter 7 you said what you like with Ich finde es gut, dass … Today you say politely what you do not like.
steps: You already know: the dass-clause with the verb at the END (Ich finde es gut, dass wir einen Putzplan machen) and Könnten Sie bitte …? from lesson 4.
New today: complaints with dass and a Wo? or Wohin? phrase, the Perfekt inside the dass-clause, and a polite complaint in four steps.
By the end you can: complain politely, ask for a change, and react well when someone complains to you.

examples.de: Ich finde es gut, dass wir einen Putzplan machen.
examples.en: I think it's good that we're making a cleaning rota.

examples.de: Es stört mich, dass die Schuhe im Hausflur stehen.
examples.en: It bothers me that the shoes are in the hallway.
examples.why: New today: a polite complaint with dass.

examples.de: Könnten Sie sie bitte in den Schrank stellen?
examples.en: Could you put them in the cupboard, please?
examples.why: From lesson 4: the request after the complaint.

cards.more: Picture two neighbours on the stairs. One says: Your shoes are in my way! The other hears an attack. Try another way: Es stört mich, dass die Schuhe im Hausflur stehen. The problem is the same, but now the sentence talks about a feeling, not about a bad person. That is why German speakers like the frame Es stört mich, dass …. It names what bothers you, not who is guilty. Today you learn this frame, and how to ask for one small change.

cards.title: A complaint in four steps
cards.body: A polite complaint has four steps. Greet: Guten Tag, Frau Weber. Name the problem: Die Musik war gestern zu laut. Say how you feel: Es stört mich, dass … Ask for a change: Könnten Sie bitte …? Other frames: Ich finde es nicht gut, dass … Ich ärgere mich, dass … Schade, dass …
cards.lead: The intro showed the problems in the house. This card gives the plan for every complaint: four short steps and four sentence frames you can start with.

examples.de: Guten Tag, Frau Weber.
examples.en: Good afternoon, Frau Weber.

examples.de: Die Musik war gestern zu laut.
examples.en: The music was too loud yesterday.

examples.de: Es stört mich, dass der Müll vor der Tür liegt.
examples.en: It bothers me that the rubbish is in front of the door.

examples.de: Könnten Sie den Müll bitte in den Mülleimer werfen?
examples.en: Could you put the rubbish in the bin, please?

deeper.text: If you are really angry, you can say: Ich möchte mich beschweren. That means I want to complain, and it sounds serious, like at a hotel desk. With neighbours, start softer with Es stört mich, dass … The reflexive mich stays after möchte, and beschweren goes to the end like every infinitive after a modal.

example.de: Ich möchte mich beschweren.
example.en: I would like to complain.

cards.more: A complaint is like a recipe with four ingredients: a greeting, the problem, your feeling, a small wish. If one is missing, it tastes wrong. Without the greeting it is rude, without the wish nobody knows what to do. Count them on your fingers: Guten Tag (1), Die Musik war zu laut (2), Es stört mich, dass … (3), Könnten Sie bitte …? (4). English speakers do the same with 'Sorry to bother you, but …'. Practise with one real problem from your day, three times, out loud.

rows: Es stört mich, dass der Müll vor der Tür liegt.
Ich finde es nicht gut, dass …
Ich finde es nicht gut, dass die Musik so laut ist.
Ich ärgere mich, dass die Schuhe im Hausflur stehen.
Schade, dass du keine Zeit hast.

steps: Greet: Guten Tag, Frau Weber.
Name the problem: Die Musik war gestern zu laut.
Say how you feel: Es stört mich, dass …
Ask for a change: Könnten Sie bitte …?

cards.title: dass + a Wo? phrase: the verb goes last
cards.body: Many complaints are about where something is. Inside the dass-clause you use a Wo? phrase with the dative and the verb stehen or liegen at the very END: Es stört mich, dass die Schuhe im Hausflur stehen. The subject comes right after dass.
cards.lead: You have the four steps. Now look closely at step three: the dass-clause. This card shows complaints about where things are, with a Wo? phrase and stehen or liegen at the end.

examples.de: Es stört mich, dass die Schuhe im Hausflur stehen.
examples.en: It bothers me that the shoes are standing in the hallway.

examples.de: Ich finde es nicht gut, dass das Fahrrad im Treppenhaus steht.
examples.en: I don't think it's good that the bike is in the stairwell.

examples.de: Es stört mich, dass der Müll vor der Tür liegt.
examples.en: It bothers me that the rubbish is lying in front of the door.

deeper.text: Why dative here? Nobody moves the shoes in this sentence. They just stand there, so you ask Wo? and use the dative: im Hausflur, vor der Tür. The dass does not change the case at all. It only changes the place of the verb. Upright things stehen, flat things liegen, as in lesson 2.

example.de: Es stört mich, dass die Jacke auf der Treppe liegt.
example.en: It bothers me that the jacket is lying on the stairs.

cards.more: Imagine the dass-clause as a small room with the last seat at the back. The verb must take the last seat. Everyone else sits down first: dass (the door), die Schuhe (who), im Hausflur (where), and last of all stehen. In English the verb stays near the subject: 'that the shoes are in the hallway'. In German it travels to the back. So say the place first, then the verb, then stop: dass die Schuhe im Hausflur stehen.

cards.title: dass + the Perfekt and a Wohin? phrase
cards.body: Sometimes you complain about what someone did. Then the Perfekt goes into the dass-clause: the participle comes first, and haben goes to the very END. The person moved something, so the place phrase is Wohin? with the accusative: Es stört mich, dass Sie die Kiste in den Hausflur gestellt haben.
cards.lead: On the last card things just stood somewhere. Now someone put them there. This card shows complaints about an action, with the Perfekt and a Wohin? phrase inside the dass-clause.

examples.de: Es stört mich, dass Sie die Kiste in den Hausflur gestellt haben.
examples.en: It bothers me that you have put the box in the hallway.

examples.de: Ich finde es nicht gut, dass ihr den Müll vor die Tür gelegt habt.
examples.en: I don't think it's good that you have put the rubbish in front of the door.

examples.de: Ich ärgere mich, dass Ben die Schuhe auf die Treppe gestellt hat.
examples.en: I'm annoyed that Ben has put the shoes on the stairs.

deeper.text: Compare: dass die Kiste im Hausflur steht, and dass Sie die Kiste in den Hausflur gestellt haben. The first describes where it is: Wo?, dative. The second describes the action: Wohin?, accusative. One small article tells the listener if you complain about the state or about the person who did it.

example.de: Es stört mich, dass du das Fahrrad ins Treppenhaus gestellt hast.
example.en: It bothers me that you have put the bike in the stairwell.

cards.more: Compare the same facts in two modes. In a normal sentence haben is in position 2: Sie haben die Kiste gestellt. After dass the order flips: dass Sie die Kiste gestellt haben. Both verb parts go to the back, the participle first and haben last. Practise in two steps: first say the facts (Sie die Kiste in den Hausflur gestellt), then close with haben, hast, habt or hat. The last word tells you who did it: Sie haben, du hast, ihr habt, Ben hat.
steps: Main clause: Es stört mich,
dass + subject: dass Sie
Object: die Kiste
Wohin? (accusative): in den Hausflur
Participle: gestellt
haben at the very END: haben.

cards.title: Stay polite: softeners and a request
cards.body: Small words make a complaint softer: bitte, leider, vielleicht, kurz. After the complaint, ask for a change with könnte: Es stört mich, dass die Musik so laut ist. Könnten Sie sie bitte leiser machen? To a friend: Könntest du bitte die Schuhe in den Schrank stellen?
cards.lead: Now you can say what bothers you. But how it sounds matters too. This card adds the small soft words and the polite request that should follow every complaint.

examples.de: Es stört mich, dass die Musik so laut ist.
examples.en: It bothers me that the music is so loud.

examples.de: Könnten Sie sie bitte leiser machen?
examples.en: Could you turn it down, please?

examples.de: Könntest du bitte die Schuhe in den Schrank stellen?
examples.en: Could you put the shoes in the cupboard, please?

examples.de: Hast du vielleicht kurz Zeit?
examples.en: Do you maybe have a moment?

deeper.text: Ruhezeiten: many German houses have a Hausordnung, the house rules, with quiet times. Die Mittagsruhe is often from 13 to 15 Uhr, and at night it should be quiet from 22 Uhr. If the Lautstärke is a problem, people first knock and talk. Only later do they write a note or speak to the owner.

example.de: Nach 22 Uhr ist Nachtruhe. Das steht in der Hausordnung.
example.en: After 10 p.m. it is night-time quiet. That is in the house rules.

cards.more: Imagine your words are a pillow. Bitte, leider and vielleicht make it soft, so the hard part, the complaint, does not hurt. Compare two versions. Hard: Die Musik ist laut! Soft: Die Musik war leider sehr laut. Könnten Sie sie bitte leiser machen? Both say the same thing, but the second makes the neighbour want to help. And always end with a wish, because a complaint without a wish leaves the other person guessing what to do.

rows: Die Musik war leider sehr laut.

cards.title: Words for the house: noise, rubbish, rules
cards.body: Learn the nouns with their article: der Hausflur, der Müll, der Mülleimer, der Krach, die Lautstärke, die Mittagsruhe, die Beschwerde, die Hausordnung. Two verbs: stören (to bother) and sich beschweren (to complain). Der Krach is an unpleasant noise. Die Lautstärke is how loud something is.
cards.lead: You can complain and you can answer a complaint. This card collects the words the neighbours use, so the questions only test what you have already met.

examples.de: Der Krach im Hausflur stört mich.
examples.en: The noise in the hallway bothers me.

examples.de: Der Mülleimer steht in der Küche.
examples.en: The bin is in the kitchen.

examples.de: Frau Weber hat eine Beschwerde.
examples.en: Frau Weber has a complaint.

deeper.text: Der Müll is uncountable: you say der Müll, never Mülls. Many words for rubbish are compounds with Müll: der Mülleimer is the bin, and die Mülltrennung is sorting rubbish into several bins. Germans take that seriously, so the Müll topic often appears in house rules. Der Krach has no plural either.

example.de: Der Müll muss in den Mülleimer.
example.en: The rubbish has to go in the bin.

cards.more: Sort the words into three boxes in your head. Box one is noise: der Krach, die Lautstärke. Box two is the house: der Hausflur, die Hausordnung, die Mittagsruhe. Box three is rubbish: der Müll, der Mülleimer. Then say one sentence for each box: Der Krach stört mich. Die Hausordnung hängt im Hausflur. Der Müll liegt vor der Tür. Words in boxes stay in your head longer than words in a long list.

cards.title: React to a complaint
cards.body: When someone complains to you, say sorry and fix it: Entschuldigung, das war nicht so gemeint. Das tut mir leid. Ich stelle die Schuhe sofort in den Schrank. If they are right: Stimmt, du hast recht. If you see it differently, stay polite: Ich verstehe das, aber …
cards.lead: You can complain politely. Now turn it around. This card shows what you say when the complaint is about you: say sorry, fix it, or disagree politely.

examples.de: Entschuldigung, das war nicht so gemeint.
examples.en: Sorry, I didn't mean it like that.

examples.de: Das tut mir leid. Ich stelle die Schuhe sofort in den Schrank.
examples.en: I'm sorry. I'll put the shoes in the cupboard right away.

examples.de: Stimmt, du hast recht.
examples.en: True, you're right.

examples.de: Ich verstehe das, aber die Party war vor 22 Uhr.
examples.en: I understand that, but the party was before 10 p.m.

deeper.text: Sometimes the complaint is not fair. Then you can say: Das ist nicht in Ordnung. It means that is not okay. Use it carefully, it is quite direct. A softer way is Ich verstehe das, aber … and your reason. After aber the word order is normal, because aber is in position 0.

example.de: Ich verstehe das, aber das Fahrrad steht nicht im Hausflur.
example.en: I understand that, but the bike isn't in the hallway.

cards.more: The best reaction to a complaint is short and has two parts: sorry and action. Das tut mir leid. Ich mache die Musik leiser. Say what you do in the present tense, and then really do it. If you think the complaint is not fair, you can still stay friendly: Ich verstehe das, aber … and then give your reason. In both cases listen first and do not interrupt. People forget a complaint quickly, but they remember how you answered.

cards.title: Mini dialogue: Frau Weber and Ben
cards.body: Read the dialogue. Frau Weber stops Ben on the stairs. She says du to Ben, and Ben says Sie to her. She names the problem with Es stört mich, dass … Ben says sorry and fixes it. Frau Weber thanks him.
cards.lead: Now both sides of a complaint come together. Frau Weber complains politely about Ben's music, and Ben reacts well. Notice the four steps and who says du or Sie.

examples.en: Ben, do you have a moment?

examples.de: Natürlich, Frau Weber.
examples.en: Of course, Frau Weber.

examples.de: Es stört mich, dass deine Musik so spät noch laut ist.
examples.en: It bothers me that your music is still loud so late.

examples.de: Das tut mir leid. Ich mache die Musik leiser.
examples.en: I'm sorry. I'll turn the music down.

examples.de: Danke, das ist nett.
examples.en: Thanks, that's kind.

deeper.text: Ben could also ask back politely, with Sie: Wann ist es Ihnen zu laut? And Frau Weber answers: Nach 22 Uhr, bitte. Then both know the rule. A question like this shows that Ben takes the complaint seriously. It also turns a complaint into a small agreement between neighbours.

example.de: Wann ist es Ihnen zu laut?
example.en: When is it too loud for you?

cards.more: Frau Weber is older and a neighbour, so Ben says Sie to her. She knows the four young people well, so she says du. Both are polite anyway: she asks first if he has time, and he says sorry and acts at once. Nobody shouts. Read the dialogue a second time and mark the four steps in Frau Weber's lines. Notice that her wish is missing: Ben offers the fix himself, and that is a very good reaction.

Ben: Natürlich, Frau Weber.
Problem and feeling: Es stört mich, dass …
Ben: Das tut mir leid. + the fix
Frau Weber: Danke, das ist nett.

lessons.title: Wir entscheiden: Putzplan und Zimmer
lessons.goal: Make a decision together in a WG-Treffen: suggest, vote, agree or disagree politely and report the result with Wir haben entschieden, dass …

grammar.topic: dass after vorschlagen, entscheiden and sich einigen
grammar.point: After Ich schlage vor, Wir haben entschieden or Wir haben uns geeinigt comes a comma and a dass-clause with the verb at the END. A modal goes after the infinitive (dass Anna das Fenster putzen muss); a separable verb is one word again (dass wir das Zimmer aufräumen). The dass-clause can also come first; then the main verb follows the comma: Dass Leon den Küchendienst macht, finde ich fair.
