cards.title: Before we start: from complaining to deciding
cards.body: After Frau Weber's complaint, the WG wants clear rules. Who cleans? Who does the kitchen? And who gets the free room? The four meet in the kitchen for a WG-Treffen. In lesson 5 you put a dass-clause after a feeling. Today the same clause comes after verbs of deciding.
steps: You already know: Ich bin dafür, dass wir einen Putzplan machen (A2 chapter 7) and the dass-clause with the verb at the END.
New today: Ich schlage vor, dass … and Wir haben entschieden, dass …, the WG-Treffen in five steps, voting, and Ich bin einverstanden.
By the end you can: make a suggestion, vote, agree or disagree politely, and say what the group has decided.

examples.de: Ich bin dafür, dass wir einen Putzplan machen.
examples.en: I'm in favour of us making a cleaning rota.

examples.de: Ich schlage vor, dass wir einen Putzplan machen.
examples.en: I suggest that we make a cleaning rota.
examples.why: New today: a suggestion with dass.

examples.de: Wir haben entschieden, dass Leon den Küchendienst macht.
examples.en: We have decided that Leon does kitchen duty.

cards.more: Think about the last time a group had to decide something: where to eat, who pays, who drives. Somebody suggests, the others say yes or no, and at the end one sentence says what is settled. German has a frame for each of these small jobs, and every one ends in a dass-clause. So you do not learn a new grammar rule today. You learn how to use a rule you already know in a real meeting, with people who may disagree.

cards.title: A WG-Treffen in five steps
cards.body: A WG-Treffen has five steps. Name the topic. Make a suggestion: Ich schlage vor, dass … Say yes or no: Ich bin dafür / dagegen, dass … or Ich bin einverstanden. Vote: Wir stimmen ab. Say the result: Wir haben entschieden, dass …
cards.lead: The intro showed why the WG meets. This card gives the order of the meeting, five steps, and the one sentence frame you need at each step.

examples.de: Unser Thema ist heute der Putzplan.
examples.en: Our topic today is the cleaning rota.

examples.de: Ich schlage vor, dass wir jeden Samstag putzen.
examples.en: I suggest that we clean every Saturday.

examples.de: Ich bin einverstanden.
examples.en: I agree.

examples.de: Wir stimmen jetzt ab.
examples.en: We'll vote now.

deeper.text: Vorschlagen and abstimmen are separable. In a normal main clause the prefix goes to the end: Wir stimmen ab. Ich schlage vor. When the dass-clause follows, the prefix vor stays before the comma: Ich schlage vor, dass … The nouns are der Vorschlag, a suggestion, and die Abstimmung, the vote. Einverstanden never changes its ending.

example.de: Die Abstimmung ist am Montag.
example.en: The vote is on Monday.

cards.more: A meeting is like a short road with five stops. Stop one: what are we talking about? Stop two: one idea. Stop three: everyone says yes or no. Stop four: hands up, we count. Stop five: the result. Learn one sentence for each stop and the meeting runs by itself. In English you may say 'I propose', 'I'm in favour' and 'The motion is carried'. German is simpler: schlage vor, bin dafür, stimmen ab, haben entschieden.
steps: Thema nennen: Unser Thema ist …
Vorschlag machen: Ich schlage vor, dass …
dafür / dagegen sagen: Ich bin dafür. / Ich bin einverstanden.
abstimmen: Wir stimmen ab.
Ergebnis sagen: Wir haben entschieden, dass …

cards.title: dass after vorschlagen and entscheiden
cards.body: After vorschlagen and entscheiden comes a comma and a dass-clause with the verb at the END. Vorschlagen is often in the present: Ich schlage vor, dass … Entscheiden is usually in the Perfekt, because the decision is finished: Wir haben entschieden, dass … The same with vorschlagen: Mira hat vorgeschlagen, dass …
cards.lead: You know the five steps. Now look at the two key verbs, vorschlagen and entscheiden, and how the dass-clause follows them in the present and in the Perfekt.

examples.de: Ich schlage vor, dass wir einen Putzplan machen.
examples.en: I suggest that we make a cleaning rota.

examples.de: Wir haben entschieden, dass Leon den Küchendienst macht.
examples.en: We have decided that Leon does kitchen duty.

examples.de: Mira hat vorgeschlagen, dass wir am Samstag das Zimmer aufräumen.
examples.en: Mira suggested that we tidy the room on Saturday.

deeper.text: Look at aufräumen in the last example. In a main clause it splits: Wir räumen das Zimmer auf. In the dass-clause it comes together again at the end: dass wir das Zimmer aufräumen. This is the same rule you know from weil and wenn. The decision word itself, entschieden or vorgeschlagen, closes the main clause before the comma.

example.de: Anna hat vorgeschlagen, dass Ben die Küche aufräumt.
example.en: Anna suggested that Ben tidies the kitchen.

cards.more: Think of the main clause as a ticket and the dass-clause as the story on the back. The ticket says what kind of thing is happening: I suggest, we decided. The story says what exactly. Between them sits the comma, a small bridge. Wrong: dass Leon macht den Küchendienst. Right: dass Leon den Küchendienst macht. In English you can often drop 'that', but in German dass stays. Say the frame aloud with three different topics.

rows: dass wir am Samstag das Zimmer aufräumen.

cards.title: Modals, separable verbs and two-way phrases
cards.body: The dass-clause can hold more: a modal, or a Wohin? or Wo? phrase. With a modal, the infinitive comes first and the modal goes last: dass Anna das Fenster putzen muss. A place phrase stays in the middle: dass wir den Schrank in den Flur stellen. The decision verb stays in position 2 of the main clause.
cards.lead: On the last card the dass-clause was short. This card fills it with more: a modal at the end, and the Wo? and Wohin? phrases from this chapter in the middle.

examples.de: Wir haben entschieden, dass Anna das Fenster putzen muss.
examples.en: We have decided that Anna has to clean the window.

examples.de: Ich schlage vor, dass wir den Schrank in den Flur stellen.
examples.en: I suggest that we put the wardrobe in the hall.

examples.de: Leon findet, dass das Regal an der Wand stehen soll.
examples.en: Leon thinks that the shelf should stand against the wall.

deeper.text: The order at the end is fixed: the infinitive, then the modal. Never dass Anna muss putzen. This is the same as with weil from A2 chapter 1. The two-way phrase follows the old test: stellen moves the Schrank, so in den Flur; stehen just describes, so an der Wand. One clause can mix both ideas.

example.de: Wir haben entschieden, dass die Schuhe im Flur stehen sollen.
example.en: We have decided that the shoes should stand in the hall.

cards.more: Picture a train. The engine is dass. The last carriage is the modal: muss, soll. Just before it rides the infinitive: putzen, stehen. All the other carriages, the person, the thing and the place, ride in the middle. The engine and the last carriage never change places. For a quick check count from the back: the last word is the verb that changes (muss, soll), the second-last is the infinitive. This also works after weil and wenn.
steps: Main clause: Wir haben entschieden,
dass + subject: dass Anna
Object or place: das Fenster / an der Wand
Infinitive: putzen / stehen
Modal at the very END: muss / soll

cards.title: The Putzplan: who does what?
cards.body: A Putzplan lists the chores and who does them each week. Chores: das Bad putzen, das Fenster putzen, die Wäsche waschen, spülen, einkaufen, den Müll rausbringen (separable). Taking turns is abwechselnd. Put a chore into the decision: Wir haben entschieden, dass Ben das Bad putzt.
cards.lead: You can suggest, vote and report a decision. This card gives you the chores the WG actually decides about, so your dass-clauses have real content.

examples.de: Anna bringt jeden Montag den Müll raus.
examples.en: Anna takes the rubbish out every Monday.

examples.de: Wir haben entschieden, dass Ben das Bad putzt.
examples.en: We have decided that Ben cleans the bathroom.

examples.de: Wir spülen abwechselnd.
examples.en: We wash up in turns.

deeper.text: A chore with a noun is a small phrase: das Bad putzen, die Wäsche waschen. The noun stays in front of the verb, so in a dass-clause you get dass Ben das Bad putzt. A separable verb joins again at the end: Ich bringe den Müll raus, but dass Ben den Müll rausbringt. In everyday speech raus is short for heraus.

example.de: Es ist fair, dass Ben den Müll rausbringt.
example.en: It is fair that Ben takes the rubbish out.

cards.more: Think of the Putzplan as a table on the fridge. On the left are the chores, on the right the names. Every Monday the names move one line down, so everybody does every job once. That is what abwechselnd means: in turns. Say the rule once in German: Wir haben entschieden, dass wir abwechselnd putzen. The table on the fridge then tells the story of the whole week, and nobody has to argue about it.

cards.title: Vote and find a compromise
cards.body: To vote, ask: Wer ist dafür? Wer ist dagegen? Then: Die Mehrheit ist dafür. If nobody wins, find a compromise: Wir machen einen Kompromiss. Sich einigen means to agree together, and it is reflexive: Wir einigen uns: Anna macht den Müll, Ben spült.
cards.lead: Now the WG has suggestions on the table. This card shows how to count the votes and what to say when the group meets in the middle.

examples.de: Wer ist dafür? Wer ist dagegen?
examples.en: Who is for it? Who is against it?

examples.de: Die Mehrheit ist dafür.
examples.en: The majority is for it.

examples.de: Wir machen einen Kompromiss.
examples.en: We'll make a compromise.

examples.de: Wir einigen uns: Anna macht den Müll, Ben spült.
examples.en: We agree: Anna does the rubbish, Ben does the dishes.

deeper.text: In the Perfekt, sich einigen takes haben, and the reflexive stays right after it: Wir haben uns geeinigt. You can add a dass-clause: Wir haben uns geeinigt, dass jeder einmal pro Woche putzt. The Entscheidung, the decision, is then clear for everyone. Write it on the Putzplan, so nobody can forget it.

example.de: Wir haben uns geeinigt, dass jeder einmal pro Woche putzt.
example.en: We agreed that everyone cleans once a week.

cards.more: Voting is easy: put up your hand for yes or for no. More hands win. That is die Mehrheit, the majority. But sometimes the losing side has a good reason, so both sides give a little: that is a Kompromiss. Then you say Wir einigen uns, which means we agree, all together. English says 'we met in the middle'. Try it for your own flat: who does the bathroom, who does the kitchen? Then say the result with Wir haben uns geeinigt, dass …

cards.title: A bit further: the dass-clause can come first
cards.body: The dass-clause can also open the sentence. Then the main verb comes right after the comma, in position 2: Dass Leon den Küchendienst macht, finde ich fair. The whole dass-clause counts as position 1. This order puts the topic first. You will meet it often, but you do not need to use it yet.
cards.lead: So far the dass-clause always came second. This card shows the other order, for reading and listening: the dass-clause first, the main verb straight after the comma.

examples.de: Dass Leon den Küchendienst macht, finde ich fair.
examples.en: That Leon does kitchen duty, I find fair.

examples.de: Dass wir ein Treffen machen, finde ich gut.
examples.en: I think it's good that we're having a meeting.

examples.de: Ich finde es gut, dass wir ein Treffen machen.
examples.en: I think it's good that we're having a meeting.

deeper.text: Look at the last two examples. In the normal order you need es: Ich finde es gut, dass … When the dass-clause comes first, es disappears, because the clause itself takes its place. Then verb, then subject: finde ich. It is the same rule as after deshalb: something in position 1, verb in position 2.

example.de: Dass Ben spült, ist fair.
example.en: That Ben does the dishes is fair.

cards.more: Turn the sentence around like a coat. Normal: Ich finde es gut, dass wir ein Treffen machen. Turned: Dass wir ein Treffen machen, finde ich gut. The dass part is now at the front, and the verb finde comes right after the comma, because the whole clause counts as position 1. English can do something similar for emphasis: 'That we meet, I think, is good.' For now just recognise it when you read or hear it. You do not have to use it yet.

rows: Ich finde es fair, dass Leon den Küchendienst macht.
Dass Leon den Küchendienst macht, finde ich fair.

cards.title: Mini dialogue: the WG-Treffen
cards.body: Read the WG-Treffen. Mira leads the meeting and suggests a Casting for the free room. Ben is for it, Leon is against it and gives a reason with denn. Anna asks for a vote. Mira says the result with Wir haben entschieden, dass …
cards.lead: Now you have all the frames, so here is a complete meeting. Follow the five steps and notice how the room question becomes a decision.

examples.de: Wir haben noch ein freies Zimmer.
examples.en: We still have a free room.

examples.de: Ich schlage vor, dass wir ein Casting machen.
examples.en: I suggest that we hold a casting.

examples.de: Ich bin dagegen, denn das dauert lange.
examples.en: I'm against it, because it takes a long time.

examples.de: Dann stimmen wir ab.
examples.en: Then let's vote.

examples.de: Wir haben entschieden, dass wir am Samstag ein Casting machen.
examples.en: We have decided that we'll hold a casting on Saturday.

deeper.text: A WG-Casting is a German tradition. When a room is free, people who want it come for a short visit. The WG asks questions, shows the flat and drinks a coffee with them. Then the WG decides together. Leon is against it at first, but the Mehrheit wins, and he is einverstanden in the end.

example.de: Am Ende ist auch Leon einverstanden.
example.en: In the end Leon agrees too.

cards.more: Read it as a small play with four people. Mira suggests, Ben says yes, Leon says no and gives a reason, Anna wants a vote, and Mira says the result. Read it once as yourself and once with the roles. Then find each of the five steps and tick them off. Last, change the topic: not a casting, but a cleaning rota or a party. The frames stay the same and only the dass-clause changes. That is the whole trick of a good meeting.

lessons.title: Als wir eingezogen sind: tell the story of a move
lessons.goal: Tell what happened when you moved in, with als + Perfekt, and choose als, wenn or dass

grammar.topic: als + Perfekt in a story; position verbs in the Perfekt; als vs wenn vs dass
grammar.point: An als-clause tells one moment in the past. Its helper verb goes to the END (Als wir eingezogen sind,), and the main clause starts with its verb right after the comma (hat es geregnet). Describe the room with hat gestanden / hat gelegen / hat gehangen + dative. Wenn = every time or now/future; dass = a statement. If the als-clause comes second, the main clause keeps normal order.
grammar.oneLine: Als wir eingezogen sind, hat es geregnet.

mistake.wrong: Wenn wir eingezogen sind, hat es geregnet.
mistake.right: Als wir eingezogen sind, hat es geregnet.
mistake.why: The move happened once in the past, so you need als. Wenn is for every time, or for now and the future.

terms.meaning: a side sentence with als: one moment in the past; its verb goes to the end
the sentence part that can stand alone: hat es geregnet / Es hat geregnet
stehen, liegen, hängen, sitzen: they say where something is (Wo? + dative)

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Als ich klein war' to 'Als wir eingezogen sind'
cards.body: Every flat has a story. The four friends still laugh about the day they moved into the WG: the rain, the heavy boxes, the doorbell. You already tell stories with als and the four-part frame. Today you tell the story of a move in the Perfekt, with position verbs inside it.
steps: You already know: als for one event in the past (Als ich klein war, …) and the story frame Anfang, Problem, Höhepunkt, Ende.
New today: als-clauses with the Perfekt, hat gestanden and hat gelegen inside a story, and the choice als, wenn or dass.
By the end you can: tell the story of your first day in a new flat in five or six sentences.

examples.de: Als ich klein war, war ich oft auf dem Jahrmarkt.
examples.en: When I was little, I was often at the fair.

examples.de: Als Anna angekommen ist, hat es geregnet.
examples.en: When Anna arrived, it rained.
examples.why: You know this already: als with the Perfekt.

examples.de: Als wir eingezogen sind, hat ein Sofa im Flur gestanden.
examples.en: When we moved in, a sofa was standing in the hall.
examples.why: New today: a position verb in the Perfekt inside the story.

cards.more: Think of a photo album of the day you moved. Every als-sentence is one photo: one moment, once, in the past. A photo shows what is happening (it rained, Frau Weber rang the bell) and what the room looked like (a sofa stood in the hall). You already know both kinds of sentence. Today you stick the photos together into a little story. Then your friends see the whole day, not only one picture, and they laugh at the right moment.

cards.title: Als wir eingezogen sind: verb at the END, then the main verb
cards.body: An als-clause tells one moment in the past. Inside it, the helper verb (bin, ist, hat, sind) goes to the very END, after the participle. After the comma the main clause starts with its verb: hat, haben, war. The subject comes after that verb.
cards.lead: You know als with war and hatte. Now the moving story needs the Perfekt inside the als-clause, so this card shows where the participle and the helper verb go.

examples.de: Als wir eingezogen sind, hat es geregnet.
examples.en: When we moved in, it rained.

examples.de: Als Leon den Schrank getragen hat, hat Mira die Tür aufgemacht.
examples.en: When Leon carried the wardrobe, Mira opened the door.

examples.de: Als Ben angekommen ist, hat Anna schon gekocht.
examples.en: When Ben arrived, Anna had already cooked.

deeper.text: With war or hatte the als-clause is short: Als wir eingezogen sind, war die Wohnung leer. The main clause can use war, hatte or the Perfekt. Both clauses together form a verb, comma, verb pattern in the middle: sind, hat. That middle is a good check: if you see two verbs next to the comma, the order is right.

example.de: Als wir eingezogen sind, war die Wohnung leer.
example.en: When we moved in, the flat was empty.

cards.more: Think of als as a magnet at the back of the sentence. It pulls the helper verb (sind, hat) to the very end, behind the participle. Wrong: Als wir sind eingezogen. Right: Als wir eingezogen sind. Then comes the comma, and the next word is a verb at once: hat es geregnet. Two verbs meet at the comma, like two people shaking hands. If you see them side by side, the order is right. Say the pattern ten times with different stories.
steps: Start with Als + subject: Als wir …
Put the participle, then the helper verb at the END: … eingezogen sind,
After the comma, the verb comes first: hat …
Then the subject and the rest: … es geregnet.

cards.title: Position verbs in the story: hat gestanden, hat gelegen
cards.body: In a story you often say where things were. Use the Perfekt of the position verbs: hat gestanden, hat gelegen, hat gehangen, hat gesessen. They describe, they have no object, so the place is dative (Wo?). Never use stand, lag or hing here.
cards.lead: The als-clause sets the moment. Now the main clause describes the room at that moment, with the position verbs you learned in lessons 1 to 3, in the Perfekt.

examples.de: Als wir eingezogen sind, hat nur ein Sofa im Wohnzimmer gestanden.
examples.en: When we moved in, only a sofa was standing in the living room.

examples.de: Als ich ins Zimmer gekommen bin, hat der Teppich schon auf dem Boden gelegen.
examples.en: When I came into the room, the carpet was already lying on the floor.

examples.de: Als Mira angekommen ist, hat das Poster schon an der Wand gehangen.
examples.en: When Mira arrived, the poster was already hanging on the wall.

deeper.text: Look at ins Zimmer gekommen: kommen is movement, so ins (in das) is accusative, Wohin?. The thing that just lies or stands is dative, Wo?. One sentence can have both. Two-way rule: Wo? → dative: Der Schrank steht in der Ecke. Wohin? → accusative: Ben stellt den Schrank in die Ecke.

example.de: Als Ben den Schrank in die Ecke gestellt hat, hat der Teppich im Flur gelegen.
example.en: When Ben put the wardrobe in the corner, the carpet was lying in the hall.

cards.more: A story is like a film. Als is the moment when the camera clicks. Then the camera looks around the room: what stood there, what lay there, what hung on the wall? You say it with hat gestanden, hat gelegen, hat gehangen. These verbs only describe, so the place takes dem, der or im. Try it with your own room on your first day: Als ich eingezogen bin, hat nur ein Bett im Zimmer gestanden. Describe three things in a row.

rows: Ein Sofa hat im Flur gestanden.
Der Teppich hat auf dem Boden gelegen.
Das Poster hat an der Wand gehangen.
Die Katze hat auf der Treppe gesessen.

cards.title: als, wenn or dass?
cards.body: Ask: once or every time? Als = one moment or period in the past. Wenn = every time (Immer wenn …), or now and in the future. Dass = it gives a statement after verbs like sehen, sagen, finden. All three send the verb to the END.
cards.lead: Now you can tell one moment with als. But a story also has habits and facts. This card helps you choose between als, wenn and dass in one text.

examples.de: Als ich eingezogen bin, war ich sehr müde.
examples.en: When I moved in, I was very tired.

examples.de: Immer wenn Frau Weber geklingelt hat, habe ich aufgemacht.
examples.en: Every time Frau Weber rang the bell, I opened the door.

examples.de: Ich habe gesehen, dass die Kiste im Flur steht.
examples.en: I saw that the box is in the hall.

deeper.text: English uses when for both once and every time, so English speakers often choose wenn by mistake. A trick: if you can add 'every time' in English, use wenn. If not, and it is the past, use als. Wenn also works for the future: Wenn ich Zeit habe, helfe ich. Dass never means when.

example.de: Wenn ich Zeit habe, helfe ich dir.
example.en: When I have time, I'll help you.

cards.more: Three doors. Als: one moment, back then. Wenn: again and again, or now and later. Dass: it opens a statement after 'I saw', 'I say', 'I think'. English uses 'when' for the first two, so English speakers often pick wenn by mistake. Wrong: Wenn wir eingezogen sind, hat es geregnet. The move happened once, so: Als wir eingezogen sind. Test yourself with 'every time': if you can add it in English, wenn is right. If not, and it is the past, take als.

rows: Immer wenn Frau Weber geklingelt hat, …
Ich habe gesehen, dass die Kiste im Flur steht.

cards.title: The main clause first: Wir haben gelacht, als …
cards.body: The als-clause can also come second. Then the main clause starts normally: subject, verb. After the comma comes als, and its verb still goes to the END: als Leon das Sofa in den Flur gestellt hat. No swap after the comma.
cards.lead: You put the als-clause first so far. Sometimes the main event is more important, so it comes first. This card shows the word order when als comes after the comma.

examples.de: Wir haben gelacht, als Leon das Sofa in den Flur gestellt hat.
examples.en: We laughed when Leon put the sofa in the hall.

examples.de: Es hat geregnet, als wir eingezogen sind.
examples.en: It rained when we moved in.

examples.de: Mira hat die Tür aufgemacht, als Frau Weber geklingelt hat.
examples.en: Mira opened the door when Frau Weber rang the bell.

deeper.text: Time words make the story clear: Zuerst haben wir die Kisten getragen. Danach haben wir gekocht. Am Ende haben wir gelacht. They stand at position 1, so the verb follows at once. Mix them with als-clauses: two or three als-sentences in a story are enough. Too many sound heavy.

example.de: Zuerst haben wir die Kisten ins Haus getragen.
example.en: First we carried the boxes into the house.

cards.more: Think of a sandwich with two halves. You can put either half on top. If the als-half is on top, the next verb jumps to the front: Als …, hat es geregnet. If the als-half is at the bottom, everything stays normal: Es hat geregnet, als wir eingezogen sind. In both cases the verb inside the als-half stands last. Choose the order by what you want to stress: the thing that happened (main clause first) or the moment (als first).

rows: Als wir eingezogen sind, hat es geregnet.
Es hat geregnet, als wir eingezogen sind.
Als Frau Weber geklingelt hat, hat Mira aufgemacht.
Mira hat aufgemacht, als Frau Weber geklingelt hat.

cards.title: Moving-in words: contract, bell, building
cards.body: Verbs: ausziehen (to move out), klingeln (to ring), sich einleben (to settle in). Nouns: der Mietvertrag, die Kaution, der Briefkasten, das Türschild, die Klingel. Two kinds of building: der Altbau (old building) and der Neubau (new building). Learn each noun with its article, then tell your first day with them.
cards.lead: You can tell the day as a story. This card gives you the things that belong to a first day in a flat: papers, the bell, the letterbox, and the type of house.

deeper.text: Altbau and Neubau show how German builds words: alt + Bau (building), neu + Bau. Altbau flats often have high ceilings and wooden floors, and many people love them. The Kaution is a deposit, usually up to three months' rent. You get it back when you move out, if the flat is in good condition. Both words come up in every flat search.

cards.more: Imagine the first day in a new flat as a list on the fridge: sign the Mietvertrag, pay the Kaution, put the names on the Türschild, test the Klingel, empty the Briefkasten. Each word is a job. Say them in the order of the day, then tell it as a story with als, dann and am Abend. A list that you can see in your head is easier to remember than a column of dry words.

cards.title: Our first day: a story in four parts
cards.body: Use the frame you know: Anfang, Problem, Höhepunkt, Ende. Start with an als-sentence, add what was difficult, then the funny or big moment, then the end of the day. Time words (dann, danach, am Abend) connect the parts.
cards.lead: You can build als-sentences in both orders. Now you put them into the four-part story frame from chapter 7 and tell the whole first day in the WG.

examples.en: High point: When Frau Weber rang the bell, we all laughed.

examples.de: Am Abend haben wir Pizza gegessen.
examples.en: End: In the evening we ate pizza.

deeper.text: Why did they laugh? Frau Weber stood at the door with a cake, and Ben had a box on his head. A Höhepunkt needs a small surprise. You can say it short: Ben hat eine Kiste auf dem Kopf getragen. The Ende can be a feeling: Am Ende waren wir müde, aber glücklich.

example.de: Am Ende waren wir müde, aber glücklich.
example.en: In the end we were tired but happy.

cards.more: A story is a little hill. Anfang: you walk up. Problem: it gets hard, with rain and heavy boxes. Höhepunkt: the top, the funny moment. Ende: you walk down and rest. One or two sentences for each part are enough, and each part can start with a different small word: als, dann, plötzlich, am Abend. Think of the hill before you speak. Then you will not forget the end, and your listener knows when the story is over.

cards.title: Weißt du noch? Anna and Ben remember
cards.body: Friends often remember together. Weißt du noch? means 'Do you remember?'. Answer with Ja, und …, and add one detail. Listen for als (one moment), the Perfekt and the position verbs.
cards.lead: You can tell the four-part story alone. In real life two people tell it together, so this card shows Anna and Ben remembering their first day.

examples.en: Anna: And when Frau Weber rang the bell, you were carrying a box.

deeper.text: The dialogue goes on. Ben: Ja, die Kiste war so schwer! Anna: Und dann hat Frau Weber einen Kuchen gebracht. Ben: Immer wenn ich jetzt Kuchen esse, lache ich. Look: immer wenn for the habit now, als for the one moment back then. Both in one short talk.

example.de: Dann hat Frau Weber einen Kuchen gebracht.
example.en: Then Frau Weber brought a cake.

cards.more: Weißt du noch? is like opening a photo album together with a friend. One person shows a photo (Als wir eingezogen sind …), the other adds what they see (Ja, und der Teppich hat im Flur gelegen!). Neither of them tells the whole story alone. That makes it good speaking practice, because you only have to say one or two sentences at a time. Read the dialogue aloud with a friend, then close the book and remember your own first day together.

lessons.title: Wir feiern! Plan a party (and sentence stress)
lessons.goal: Plan a WG party (who does what, where things go), write an invitation and use sentence stress

grammar.topic: Wo? and Wohin? in a plan and its result; present tense for the future; sentence stress and melody
grammar.point: A plan moves things: stellen, legen, hängen + object, so Wohin? + accusative (auf den Balkon). The result just is there: stehen, liegen, hängen, sitzen, so Wo? + dative (auf dem Balkon). For plans, use the present with a time word: Am Samstag bringt Herr Ali den Kuchen. In speech, stress the most important or new word; yes/no questions go up, W-questions go down.
grammar.oneLine: Mira stellt die Getränke auf den Balkon. Die Getränke stehen auf dem Balkon.

mistake.wrong: Ich stelle die Getränke auf dem Balkon.
mistake.right: Ich stelle die Getränke auf den Balkon.
mistake.why: stellen has an object that you move, so the place answers Wohin? and takes the accusative: auf den Balkon.

terms.meaning: the loudest word in a sentence, usually the new or important one (der Satzakzent)
the voice going up or down at the end of a sentence
a question with a question word: wann, wo, wohin, wer, was

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Wir haben das Zimmer eingerichtet' to 'Wir feiern am Samstag'
cards.body: The free room is ready, and the WG wants to celebrate. A party needs a plan: who does what, where do the drinks go, who gets an invitation? You already know the place verbs and how to ask for a favour. Today you plan the party and learn which word in a sentence gets the stress.
steps: You already know: Wir stellen die Lampe in die Ecke. Könntest du mir helfen? and time words like am Samstag.
New today: a party plan with Wer? Was? Wohin? Wann?, an invitation, and sentence stress (Satzakzent).
By the end you can: plan a party, write a short invitation and stress the important word.

examples.de: Wir stellen die Lampe in die Ecke.
examples.en: We put the lamp in the corner.
examples.why: You know this already: Wohin? + accusative.

examples.de: Könntest du mir helfen?
examples.en: Could you help me?
examples.why: You know this already: a polite request.

examples.de: Wir feiern am Samstag in unserer WG.
examples.en: We are having a party on Saturday in our flat share.
examples.why: New today: the present tense for a plan.

cards.more: A party is like a little play. Everyone needs a role (Mira: drinks, Ben: garland), every thing needs a place, and the invitation is the poster. And when you talk, one word in each sentence shines brightest: that is the stress. Today you do all four jobs at once: you plan with the Wohin? side of the two-way rule, you describe the result with the Wo? side, you write the invitation, and you make your sentences sound German.

cards.title: The plan: who puts what where?
cards.body: For a plan in German, use the present tense with a time word: Am Samstag stellt Mira die Getränke auf den Balkon. Each job moves something somewhere, so the place answers Wohin? and takes the accusative: auf den Balkon, an die Wand.
cards.lead: The room is ready. Now the WG writes the party plan, and every job moves a thing to a place: that is the Wohin? side of the two-way rule.

examples.de: Mira stellt die Getränke auf den Balkon.
examples.en: Mira puts the drinks on the balcony.

examples.de: Ben hängt die Girlande an die Wand.
examples.en: Ben hangs the garland on the wall.

examples.de: Am Samstag lädt Anna die Gäste ein.
examples.en: On Saturday Anna invites the guests.

deeper.text: German does not need a future form for a plan: the present plus a time word is normal. Am Samstag bringt Herr Ali den Kuchen. Um acht baut Leon die Lautsprecher auf. The time word at position 1 pushes the subject behind the verb. Two-way rule: Wo? → dative: Der Schrank steht in der Ecke. Wohin? → accusative: Ben stellt den Schrank in die Ecke.

example.de: Um acht baut Leon die Lautsprecher auf.
example.en: At eight Leon sets up the speakers.

cards.more: A plan is a to-do list with arrows. Each arrow goes from a person to a place: Mira, the drinks, onto the balcony. An arrow means movement, so you say auf den, an die, in die. You also do not need a special future tense. English says 'will' or 'is going to'. German simply uses the present and adds a time word: am Samstag, um acht, schon morgen. The time word tells everybody that it is a plan, not something happening now.

cards.title: During the party: where is everything?
cards.body: When the work is done, things just are somewhere. Now use stehen, liegen, hängen and sitzen: no object, so the place answers Wo? and takes the dative: auf dem Balkon, an der Wand, im Wohnzimmer.
cards.lead: The plan moved everything. Now the party starts, and you describe the result: the same things, but now they stand, hang and sit, so you switch to the dative.

examples.de: Die Getränke stehen auf dem Balkon.
examples.en: The drinks are on the balcony.

examples.de: Die Girlande hängt an der Wand.
examples.en: The garland is hanging on the wall.

examples.de: Die Gäste sitzen im Wohnzimmer.
examples.en: The guests are sitting in the living room.

deeper.text: One thing, two sentences: Mira stellt die Getränke auf den Balkon (plan, movement). Die Getränke stehen auf dem Balkon (result, rest). Only the verb and the article change. Hängen is the same word in both: Ben hängt die Girlande an die Wand. Die Girlande hängt an der Wand. The object decides.

example.de: Die Lautsprecher stehen in der Ecke.
example.en: The speakers are in the corner.

cards.more: First the arrow, then the dot. Arrow: someone moves it, so auf den Balkon. Dot: it is just there, so auf dem Balkon. Imagine a photo of the party: nobody carries anything, everything stands, hangs or sits. So the photo needs the dative. Wrong: Die Getränke stehen auf den Balkon. Right: Die Getränke stehen auf dem Balkon. A quick check: can you add a person who carries it? No person, no arrow, so dative.

cards.body: Learn the party words with their article: die Girlande, der Luftballon, der Lautsprecher, die Deko, das Besteck. Die Chips is plural only. The host is der Gastgeber or die Gastgeberin. Verbs: aufbauen (to set up) and abbauen (to take down) are opposites, and verteilen means to hand out.
cards.lead: You can plan and describe the party. This card gives you the words for the things and the jobs, so you can fill your plan with real content.

deeper.text: Everyday German often shortens long words: die Dekoration becomes die Deko, die Universität becomes die Uni. The short word keeps the article. Aufbauen and abbauen are opposites: auf- builds up, ab- takes away. Both are separable, so the prefix goes to the end of the sentence.

example.de: Wir bauen alles ab.
example.en: We take everything down.

cards.more: Imagine the party as three boxes. In box one are the things you hang or put up: die Girlande, der Luftballon, die Deko. In box two are the things for eating: das Besteck, die Chips. In box three are the people and the jobs: der Gastgeber, aufbauen, abbauen, verteilen. Pull one word from each box and make a sentence: Der Gastgeber verteilt das Besteck. Boxes help you find the word fast when you speak.

cards.title: The invitation: Wann? Wo? Was mitbringen?
cards.body: A good invitation answers four questions: Wann? Wo? Wie lange? Was mitbringen? Write to Frau Weber and Herr Ali with Sie. Start with Liebe Frau Weber, or Lieber Herr Ali, and continue with a small letter. End with Viele Grüße, a new line and your name: no comma after the closing.
cards.lead: Everything has its place. Now the guests need to know about it, so you write an invitation and learn how to answer one.

examples.en: Gladly, I'm coming!

deeper.text: Answers: say yes with Gern, ich komme! or Ich komme gern. Say no politely: Leider kann ich nicht, ich muss arbeiten. Add a nice line: Wir freuen uns auf Sie (or auf dich). Frau Weber writes back with du to the young four: Danke, ich bringe einen Salat mit.

example.de: Leider kann ich nicht, ich muss arbeiten.
example.en: Unfortunately I can't, I have to work.

cards.more: An invitation is a small map: when (Saturday, 7 pm), where (our WG), how long (until midnight), what to bring (a salad?). If one of the four is missing, the guest has to write back and ask. Here is Mira's invitation, with Sie: Liebe Frau Weber, (new line) wir feiern am Samstag um 19 Uhr in unserer WG. Kommen Sie auch? (new line) Viele Grüße (new line) Mira. Note the comma after the greeting, and none after the closing.

cards.title: Sentence stress: the important word is loud
cards.body: In every sentence one word carries the stress (der Satzakzent): the most important or new word. Little words like der, die, in, ich stay short and quiet. Change the stress and the meaning changes: stress on feiern means we celebrate and do not work; stress on Samstag means Saturday, not Sunday.
cards.lead: You can now say the plan. Now you learn how to say it like a German: which word in the sentence is loud, and why it can change what you mean.

examples.de: Wir feiern am Samstag.
examples.en: We celebrate on Saturday. (stress on Samstag: not Sunday)

examples.de: Wir feiern am Samstag.
examples.en: We celebrate on Saturday. (stress on feiern: we don't work)

examples.de: Nicht in die Küche, sondern in den Flur.
examples.en: Not into the kitchen, but into the hall. (stress on Küche and Flur)

deeper.text: In a normal sentence with no contrast, the stress falls on the last important word: in Mira stellt die Getränke auf den Balkon it is Balkon. When you correct someone, you stress the new information: Nicht Ben, Leon macht den Salat (stress on Leon). This stress is often stronger than in English, so do not be shy.

example.de: Leon macht den Salat.
example.en: Leon makes the salad. (stress on Leon, not Ben)

cards.more: Picture a torch. In each sentence you shine it on one word. That word is louder, a little higher and a bit longer. The little words stay in the dark. Where the torch shines, there is the news. English does this too: 'I said Saturday, not Sunday.' Try it: say Wir feiern am Samstag three times and shine the torch on a different word each time. Listen to how the meaning moves with the light.

rows: Nicht in die Küche, sondern in den Flur.

cards.title: Questions and melody: up or down?
cards.body: Yes/no questions go up at the end: Kommst du auch? ↗. W-questions go down: Wann feiern wir? ↘, Wohin stellen wir die Getränke? ↘. In a W-question the stress is usually on the question word or on the last important word.
cards.lead: Stress makes one word loud. The melody is the line of the whole sentence, and in questions it tells the listener what kind of answer you want.

examples.de: Kommst du auch?
examples.en: Are you coming too? ↗ (voice goes up)

examples.de: Wann feiern wir?
examples.en: When are we celebrating? ↘ (voice goes down)

examples.de: Wohin stellen wir die Getränke?
examples.en: Where do we put the drinks? ↘ (stress on Wohin or Getränke)

deeper.text: A W-question with the voice going up sounds surprised or like you did not hear: Wann feiern wir? ↗ = Sorry, when? A statement with the voice going up becomes a question: Du kommst auch? ↗ That is very common in speech. Try both with the video for this lesson.

example.de: Du kommst auch?
example.en: You're coming too? ↗ (a statement as a question)

cards.more: Melody is a hill or a slide. Yes/no questions climb a hill at the end: Kommst du auch? ↗. W-questions slide down: Wann feiern wir? ↘. Draw a small arrow over every question you practise in your notes. English does the same for yes/no questions, so you already feel it. The new part is the W-question, where English speakers often go up. In German, down is normal, and up sounds like 'Sorry, what did you say?'

cards.title: Wer macht was? Mira, Anna and Leon plan
cards.body: Listen to the plan in the WG. Questions with Wer? and Wohin?, short answers (Ich! An die Wand.) and stress on the new word. Short answers drop the verb: Wohin? – An die Wand. The case stays the same as in the full sentence.
cards.lead: You know the plan, the places, the invitation and the melody. Now everything comes together in a real planning talk in the kitchen.

examples.de: Wer stellt die Getränke auf den Balkon?
examples.en: Mira: Who puts the drinks on the balcony?

examples.de: Und wohin hängen wir die Girlande?
examples.en: Anna: And where do we hang the garland?

examples.en: Mira: On the wall, above the sofa.

deeper.text: The talk goes on. Leon: Dann stehen die Gäste nicht im Weg. Anna: Gute Idee! Und wer baut die Lautsprecher auf? Leon: Ich, am Samstag um sechs. Mira: Super, und am Sonntag bauen wir alles wieder ab. Abbauen is the opposite of aufbauen.

example.de: Am Sonntag bauen wir alles wieder ab.
example.en: On Sunday we take everything down again.

cards.more: A planning talk is ping-pong: a question flies over (Wer? Wohin?), a short answer comes back (Ich! An die Wand.). Keep the answers short, but keep den, die, das right, because the case stays the same as in the full sentence. Read the dialogue aloud and listen to the melody: the W-questions slide down, and the answers are short and firm. Then close the book and plan a party with a friend: choose three jobs and three places.

lessons.title: Nach der Party: report experiences and write a story
lessons.goal: Report what happened at and after the party in the Perfekt and write a short story with a five-step plan

grammar.topic: a connected report in the Perfekt with als, dass, weil, deshalb, trotzdem; writing in five steps
grammar.point: Tell the story in the Perfekt: hat gespült, hat weggeräumt, ist kaputtgegangen, hat sich entschuldigt. als, dass and weil send the verb to the END. deshalb and trotzdem stand at position 1 with the verb right after them. Plan your text in five steps: collect, order (Anfang, Problem, Höhepunkt, Ende), connect, check the verbs, read aloud.

cards.title: Before we start: from planning to telling
cards.body: The party is over. The flat is a mess, everyone is tired, and Ben wants to hear everything. Yesterday you planned the party in the present tense. Today you tell what happened, in the Perfekt, with all the connectors you know, and you learn five steps for writing your own story.
steps: You already know: Als wir eingezogen sind, hat es geregnet. Zuerst haben wir die Girlande aufgehängt. weil, deshalb and trotzdem.
New today: words for the morning after (spülen, wegräumen, kaputtgehen), a longer report and a five-step writing plan.
By the end you can: write a short story of eight to ten sentences about a party or a day.

examples.en: When we moved in, it rained.

examples.en: First we hung up the garland.

examples.en: A glass broke.

cards.more: Telling a story is like putting a puzzle together. The pieces are short sentences in the Perfekt. The connectors (als, weil, deshalb, trotzdem) are the edges that hold the pieces together, and the five steps are the picture on the box lid. Yesterday you only planned. Today you look back, so everything that happened gets a participle at the end. After this lesson you can tell a friend what happened at a party and write it down in ten sentences.

cards.title: The morning after: spülen, wegräumen, kaputtgehen
cards.body: After a party you say what you did: Wir haben das Geschirr gespült. Leon hat die Scherben weggeräumt. Kaputtgehen means to break by itself, so it takes sein: Ein Glas ist kaputtgegangen. Sich entschuldigen is reflexive: Ben hat sich entschuldigt.
cards.lead: The party plan was in the present. Now the party is over, so you need the Perfekt of the clean-up verbs before you can tell the whole story.

examples.de: Wir haben das Geschirr gespült.
examples.en: We washed the dishes.

examples.de: Leon hat die Scherben weggeräumt.
examples.en: Leon cleared away the broken pieces.

examples.de: Ein Glas ist kaputtgegangen.
examples.en: A glass broke.

deeper.text: Weggeräumt and kaputtgegangen are separable verbs: the ge sits between the prefix and the verb (weg-ge-räumt, kaputt-ge-gangen). Kaputtgehen takes sein because the glass changes its state and nobody does it on purpose. If someone breaks it, German often says: Ben hat ein Glas kaputt gemacht.

example.de: Ben hat sich bei Frau Weber entschuldigt.
example.en: Ben apologised to Frau Weber.

cards.more: Imagine a messy kitchen on Sunday. Each verb is one job: spülen (wash the dishes), wegräumen (put away), sich entschuldigen (say sorry). Kaputtgehen is the accident that made the mess. Look at the helper verb: when a person does a job, you use haben (hat gespült, hat weggeräumt). When something just happens to a thing, you use sein (ist kaputtgegangen). Ask yourself: does somebody do it, or does it just happen? That decides haben or sein.

cards.title: After the party: things and leftovers
cards.body: Learn the nouns with their article: das Geschirr (dishes, no plural), die Scherbe, der Fleck, der Rest, der Müllsack. Übrig means left over and takes no ending. Use these words in the Perfekt report: Wir haben das Geschirr gespült. Es ist noch Kuchen übrig.
cards.lead: You can name the jobs of the morning after. This card adds the things you find in the flat: dishes, broken glass, stains and leftovers.

deeper.text: Die Scherbe is one piece of broken glass, die Scherben are the pieces on the floor. A German saying goes: Scherben bringen Glück, broken pieces bring luck. People say it when a glass breaks at a party, to make the person feel better. Der Rest has a plural too: die Reste means leftovers.

example.de: Die Scherben liegen auf dem Boden.
example.en: The broken pieces are lying on the floor.

cards.more: Imagine the kitchen on Sunday morning and say what you see. Das Geschirr steht auf dem Tisch. Die Scherben liegen auf dem Boden. Ein Fleck ist auf dem Teppich. Ein Rest Kuchen ist übrig. Each sentence uses a word from this card and a position verb from this chapter. That is how the topic words and the grammar stick together, and you can repeat it every morning with your own kitchen.

cards.title: als and dass in the report
cards.body: Use als for one moment of the party: Als die Party zu Ende war, haben wir aufgeräumt. Use dass after verbs like sehen or finden: Ich habe gesehen, dass ein Fleck auf dem Teppich war. In both, the verb goes to the END.
cards.lead: You have the clean-up verbs. Now you connect them: als gives the moment, dass gives what you saw or think, just as in lesson 7, but now in a party report.

examples.de: Als die Party zu Ende war, haben wir aufgeräumt.
examples.en: When the party was over, we tidied up.

examples.de: Als der letzte Gast gegangen ist, war es zwei Uhr.
examples.en: When the last guest left, it was two o'clock.

examples.de: Ich habe gesehen, dass ein Fleck auf dem Teppich war.
examples.en: I saw that there was a stain on the carpet.

deeper.text: A dass-clause can also give a feeling about now: Ich finde es schade, dass die Party vorbei ist. The main clause is present (Ich finde), the dass-clause is present too. In a report you mix: the story in the Perfekt, your feelings now in the present. That makes the text alive.

example.de: Ich finde es schade, dass die Party vorbei ist.
example.en: I think it's a pity that the party is over.

cards.more: Wrong: Als die Party zu Ende war, wir haben aufgeräumt. After the comma the verb comes first: haben wir aufgeräumt. Think: verb, comma, verb. war, haben. Two verbs stand next to the comma like two neighbours. Dass works as a window into your thoughts: Ich habe gesehen, dass … is something you saw, and Ich finde es schade, dass … is something you feel. English often hides 'that' (I saw the stain was big), but German always shows it, and always with a comma before it.

cards.title: weil, deshalb, trotzdem: reasons and surprises
cards.body: Weil gives the reason, verb at the END: …, weil die Musik laut war. Deshalb gives the result, trotzdem a surprise; both stand at position 1 and the verb comes right after: Deshalb haben Scherben auf dem Boden gelegen. Trotzdem haben wir getanzt.
cards.lead: als and dass tell moments and facts. A good report also explains why things happened and what followed, so this card brings back weil, deshalb and trotzdem.

examples.de: Wir waren müde. Trotzdem haben wir alles weggeräumt.
examples.en: We were tired. Still, we cleared everything away.

examples.de: Ein Glas ist kaputtgegangen. Deshalb haben Scherben auf dem Boden gelegen.
examples.en: A glass broke. That's why broken pieces were lying on the floor.

examples.de: Frau Weber hat geklingelt, weil die Musik zu laut war.
examples.en: Frau Weber rang the bell because the music was too loud.

deeper.text: Weil and deshalb say the same thing from two sides. Weil: reason in the side sentence. Deshalb: reason first, then the result as a new main sentence. Trotzdem means: the reason is there, but the result is the opposite. Note: liegen takes haben in the Perfekt here (hat gelegen), as you learned in lesson 2.

example.de: Die Musik war laut. Deshalb hat Frau Weber geklingelt.
example.en: The music was loud. That's why Frau Weber rang the bell.

cards.more: Weil, deshalb and trotzdem tell the same story from different sides. Imagine a seesaw. Weil: the reason is in the side sentence, and the verb goes to the end. Deshalb: the reason comes first, then the result jumps to the front. Trotzdem: the result does not match the reason, like a surprise. Wrong: Deshalb ich bin müde. Right: Deshalb bin ich müde. Deshalb and trotzdem take the first seat, so the verb sits right next to them.

cards.title: Writing a story in five steps
cards.body: Good writers plan. 1 Collect words and ideas. 2 Put them in order: Anfang, Problem, Höhepunkt, Ende. 3 Connect them with zuerst, dann, als, weil, deshalb, trotzdem. 4 Check the verbs: haben or sein, verb at the END after als, dass, weil. 5 Read it aloud and fix it.
cards.lead: You now have the words and the connectors. Before you write your own story, here is a plan in five steps that works for every text, at A2 and in the exam.

examples.de: Zuerst haben wir die Girlande aufgehängt.
examples.en: Step 3, connect: First we hung up the garland.

examples.de: Dann sind die Gäste gekommen.
examples.en: Step 3, connect: Then the guests came.

examples.de: Ein Glas ist kaputtgegangen.
examples.en: Step 4, check: kaputtgehen takes sein.

deeper.text: Step 4 is where most points are won. Use a checklist: Is the helper right (sein for gehen, kommen, kaputtgehen; haben for most others)? Is the participle at the end? After als, dass, weil: is the verb at the END? After deshalb and trotzdem: is the verb right after? Ten sentences take about two minutes to check.

example.de: Als die Gäste gekommen sind, haben wir getanzt.
example.en: When the guests came, we danced.

cards.more: Building a story is like cooking. Step 1: get the ingredients, which are words and ideas. Step 2: put them in order. Step 3: mix them with connectors. Step 4: taste, which means check the verbs. Step 5: serve, which means read it aloud. Cooks never skip tasting, and writers should not skip step 4, because that is where most mistakes are found. Use the little checklist on this card for every text you write, at home and in an exam.
steps: Collect words and ideas (Party, Girlande, Glas, Scherben, müde).
Put them in order: Anfang, Problem, Höhepunkt, Ende.
Connect: zuerst, dann, als, weil, deshalb, trotzdem.
Check the verbs: haben or sein? Verb at the END after als/dass/weil?
Read it aloud and fix it.

cards.title: A model text: Unsere Party
cards.body: Here is Mira's text about the party. Look for the four parts, the connectors and the verbs at the end. Anfang: the plan. Problem: a glass breaks and the music is loud. Höhepunkt: Herr Ali arrives. Ende: the morning after.
cards.lead: You have the five steps. Now see them in a finished text: Mira followed the steps and wrote about the WG party in about ninety words.

examples.en: On Saturday we had our first flat-share party.

deeper.text: Mira's whole text: Am Samstag haben wir unsere erste WG-Party gefeiert. Zuerst haben Ben und ich die Girlande aufgehängt. Um acht sind die Gäste gekommen. Dann ist ein Glas kaputtgegangen. Frau Weber hat geklingelt, weil die Musik zu laut war. Trotzdem haben wir getanzt. Als Herr Ali mit dem Kuchen gekommen ist, haben alle gelacht. Am Sonntag waren wir müde.

example.de: Trotzdem haben wir getanzt.
example.en: Still, we danced.

cards.more: Read the text like a detective. Find als (one moment), weil (a reason), deshalb (a result), trotzdem (a surprise). Then find every verb at the end. Put a finger on each participle and say its helper: gefeiert (haben), gekommen (sein), kaputtgegangen (sein). When you can find them all, you can write your own text. A good exercise: copy the model text and change three facts, for example the day, the gift or the person who comes late.

rows: Am Samstag haben wir unsere erste WG-Party gefeiert. Zuerst haben Ben und ich die Girlande aufgehängt.
Dann ist ein Glas kaputtgegangen. Deshalb haben Scherben auf dem Boden gelegen. Frau Weber hat geklingelt, weil die Musik zu laut war. Ben hat die Musik leiser gemacht. Trotzdem haben wir getanzt.
Als Herr Ali mit dem Kuchen gekommen ist, haben alle gelacht.
Am Sonntag waren wir müde, aber wir haben alles weggeräumt. Das war ein schöner Abend!

cards.title: Wie war die Party? Ben and Mira
cards.body: Ben went to bed early on Saturday and missed the end of the party. On Sunday morning he asks Mira. Listen for the question Wie war …?, als with the Perfekt and trotzdem. Answer a Wie war …? question with an adjective first (Super! Lustig!) and then one detail.
cards.lead: You have read Mira's text. Now hear the same story in a real conversation: spoken reports are shorter and use more short answers.

examples.de: Wie war die Party?
examples.en: Ben: How was the party?

examples.de: Super! Als Herr Ali gekommen ist, haben alle gelacht.
examples.en: Mira: Great! When Herr Ali came, everybody laughed.

examples.de: Wir alle. Trotzdem liegt noch Müll im Flur.
examples.en: Mira: All of us. Still, there's rubbish lying in the hall.

deeper.text: The talk goes on. Ben: Und wer hat aufgeräumt? Mira: Wir alle. Trotzdem liegt noch Müll im Flur. Ben: Kein Problem, ich bringe die Müllsäcke runter. Mira: Danke! Und es gibt noch Reste vom Kuchen. Look: the report is Perfekt, but what you see now is present: liegt noch, gibt noch.

example.de: Es gibt noch Reste vom Kuchen.
example.en: There are still leftovers of the cake.

cards.more: A morning-after chat is like a short news show. Ben asks the headline (Wie war die Party?). Mira gives a one-word answer (Super!) and one story (Als Herr Ali gekommen ist, …). Then they talk about now: the mess in the hall. Notice that spoken German is shorter than written German: only short pieces, and they are the same pieces as in the model text. Practise it with a friend: one asks, one tells, and then you swap.

rows: Super! Als Herr Ali gekommen ist, haben alle gelacht.
Wir alle. Trotzdem liegt noch Müll im Flur.
Kein Problem, ich bringe die Müllsäcke runter.
Danke! Und es gibt noch Reste vom Kuchen.

grammar.topic: Wo? and Wohin? with town places and adjectives; hier/dort vs hierhin/dorthin; a city presentation in five steps
grammar.point: Places where something is take Wo? + dative (am Stadtrand, in der schönen Altstadt); places you go to take Wohin? + accusative (ins Einkaufszentrum, in die schöne Altstadt). Hier and dort answer Wo?, hierhin and dorthin answer Wohin?. A city presentation has five steps: name, size, places, what you do, opinion.

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich wohne in der Altstadt' to 'Dorthin gehe ich gern'
cards.body: Sooner or later someone asks: Where do you live? What is your town like? Where do you go at the weekend? Today you answer with real places of a town, with Wo? and Wohin?, and with two small new words that point: hierhin and dorthin. At the end you present your own Viertel in five steps.
steps: You already know: Ich gehe in die Stadt (Wohin?) and Ich bin in der Stadt (Wo?) from A2 chapter 5, and zum Bahnhof, links von from chapter 7.
New today: hierhin and dorthin for Wohin?, town places like der Marktplatz and das Einkaufszentrum, and a city presentation in five steps.
By the end you can: present your town or Viertel: where things are, where you go and what you think of it.

examples.de: Ich bin in der Stadt.
examples.en: I am in town.
examples.why: You know this already: Wo? + dative.

examples.de: Dorthin gehe ich gern.
examples.en: I like going there.

cards.more: Think of a town as a map with pins. Some sentences say where a pin is (Wo?), some say where you walk to (Wohin?). You already know this from in der Stadt and in die Stadt. Today the map gets more pins: a market square, a shopping centre, a village nearby. And you learn two little arrows, hierhin and dorthin, that point to a goal. At the end Mira presents her Viertel, and you can copy her five steps for your own town.

cards.title: Places in a town
cards.body: A town has many places: der Ort (place, small town), das Dorf (village), der Vorort (suburb), der Marktplatz and das Einkaufszentrum. The old rule works here too: a place where something is takes Wo? + dative, a place you go to takes Wohin? + accusative.
cards.lead: You know die Altstadt, der Stadtteil and der Stadtrand. This card adds five new town places and puts each one in the Wo? and the Wohin? column.

examples.de: Das Einkaufszentrum liegt am Stadtrand.
examples.en: The shopping centre is on the edge of town.

examples.de: Wir gehen ins Einkaufszentrum.
examples.en: We are going to the shopping centre.

examples.de: Der Marktplatz ist in der Mitte.
examples.en: The market square is in the middle.

deeper.text: Auf den Marktplatz means you walk onto the square itself. Zum Marktplatz means you go towards it, maybe to meet someone there. Zu always takes the dative, even with movement, so it never changes: zum Marktplatz, zur Altstadt, zum Einkaufszentrum. Only the nine two-way prepositions switch between Wo? and Wohin?.

example.de: Ich fahre zum Einkaufszentrum.
example.en: I'm driving to the shopping centre.

cards.more: Picture a pin and an arrow. A pin sits still: Das Einkaufszentrum liegt am Stadtrand (Wo?, dative). An arrow moves: Wir gehen ins Einkaufszentrum (Wohin?, accusative). It is the same rule as in your flat: Wo? → dative: Der Schrank steht in der Ecke. Wohin? → accusative: Ben stellt den Schrank in die Ecke. The town is just a bigger room. 1. Ask Wo? or Wohin? 2. Wo? gives dem/der/dem. 3. Wohin? gives den/die/das. Then say it aloud: Der Marktplatz ist in der Mitte. Wir gehen auf den Marktplatz.

cards.title: hier and dort, hierhin and dorthin
cards.body: Hier (here) and dort (there) answer Wo?. For Wohin? German adds -hin, a little arrow to a goal: hierhin (to here) and dorthin (to there). So: Wo ist der Park? Dort. But: Wohin gehst du? Dorthin. Da and dahin mean the same; you will hear them a lot.
cards.lead: Now you know the town places. This card gives you short pointing words for them: hier and dort for Wo?, hierhin and dorthin for Wohin?.

examples.de: Wo ist der Park? Dort.
examples.en: Where is the park? Over there.

examples.de: Wohin gehst du? Dorthin.
examples.en: Where are you going? Over there.

examples.de: Wir stellen den Sessel hierhin.
examples.en: We'll put the armchair here.

deeper.text: Hin always points away from you, towards a goal. That is why it appears in Wohin? and in hierhin and dorthin: they answer the same question. A quick check: if you can ask Wohin?, add -hin. If you can only ask Wo?, use hier or dort. Da and dahin are the everyday middle words; you may simply use dort and dorthin.

example.de: Wo ist die Katze? Da, auf dem Fensterbrett.
example.en: Where is the cat? There, on the windowsill.

cards.more: Think of hin as an arrow sticker. Hier and dort are dots on the map: Die Katze sitzt dort (Wo?). Hierhin and dorthin are dots with an arrow: Stell den Sessel hierhin! (Wohin?). The question tells you whether you need the sticker. 1. Wohin gehst du? → Dorthin. 2. Wo wohnst du? → Dort. 3. Wohin stellen wir den Sessel? → Hierhin. A common mistake is Ich gehe dort. Gehen moves, so it needs the arrow: Ich gehe dorthin.

cards.title: Town places with adjectives
cards.body: Add an adjective and the case still comes from the verb: wohnen = Wo? = dative, so in der schönen Altstadt. Gehen or ziehen = Wohin? = accusative, so in die schöne Altstadt. The verb gives the case, the ending shows it.
cards.lead: You can say in der Altstadt and in die Altstadt. This card adds an adjective in the middle and shows that its ending follows the same Wo?/Wohin? choice.

examples.de: Wir wohnen in der schönen Altstadt.
examples.en: We live in the beautiful old town.

examples.de: Wir gehen in die schöne Altstadt.
examples.en: We are going to the beautiful old town.

examples.de: Mira wohnt in einem ruhigen Viertel.
examples.en: Mira lives in a quiet neighbourhood.

deeper.text: After im and am the ending is -en too, because im is in dem: im großen Park, am kleinen Marktplatz. And watch ein in the accusative: das Viertel becomes ein ruhiges Viertel, with -es on the adjective, because ein itself shows no gender. Anna zieht in ein ruhiges Viertel, but Mira wohnt in einem ruhigen Viertel.

example.de: Anna zieht in ein ruhiges Viertel.
example.en: Anna is moving to a quiet neighbourhood.

cards.more: Think of a train: the verb is the engine, the article is the first wagon, the adjective is the second. The engine decides where the train goes, and the wagons follow. 1. Find the verb: wohnen (Wo?) or gehen (Wohin?). 2. Choose the article: der or die. 3. Give the adjective its ending: der schönen, die schöne. A typical mistake: Wir gehen in der Altstadt. Gehen moves, so it is Wohin?: Wir gehen in die Altstadt.

cards.title: Present a town in five steps
cards.body: A short city presentation has five steps: 1 the name and where it is, 2 the size and the people (die Einwohner = the inhabitants), 3 the places, 4 what you do where, 5 your opinion and an invitation. To compare city and country, use einerseits … andererseits.
cards.lead: Now you have places, pointing words and endings. This card puts them in order: five steps that turn single sentences into a short presentation of your town.

examples.de: Ich wohne in einem Vorort.
examples.en: I live in a suburb.

examples.de: Hier wohnen viele Einwohner.
examples.en: Many people live here.

examples.de: Am Wochenende gehe ich in den Park.
examples.en: At the weekend I go to the park.

deeper.text: Step 5 is where you show your view. Einerseits … andererseits gives both sides: one good point, one other point. Das Stadtleben is lively, a Dorf is quiet and ländlich (rural), with a lot of Natur. Both words come first in their part, so the verb comes right after them: Einerseits ist …, andererseits ist ….

example.de: Einerseits ist das Stadtleben lebendig, andererseits ist ein Dorf ruhig.
example.en: On the one hand city life is lively, on the other hand a village is quiet.

cards.more: Think of showing a friend a photo album of your town. Page 1: the name on the cover (Ich wohne in …). Page 2: how big it is (Hier wohnen viele Einwohner). Page 3: the sights (Es gibt einen Marktplatz). Page 4: you in the photos (Am Wochenende gehe ich in den Park). Page 5: a sticky note: Ich finde, dass meine Stadt schön ist. Kommt mal vorbei! Five pages, five steps, and nobody gets lost.
steps: Name and where: Ich wohne in … Das liegt …
Size and people: Hier wohnen viele Einwohner.
Places: Es gibt einen Marktplatz und ein Einkaufszentrum.
What you do where: Am Wochenende gehe ich in den Park / auf den Markt.
Opinion and invitation: Ich finde, dass … Kommt mal vorbei!

cards.title: Mira presents her Viertel
cards.body: Here is Mira's presentation in five parts. Find the five steps, the Wo? and Wohin? phrases, dorthin, one dass-clause and one weil-clause. Then read it aloud, slowly, like a real talk.
cards.lead: You know the five steps. This card shows them working together in one real presentation: Mira talks about her Viertel for about one minute.

examples.de: Dorthin fährt die Straßenbahn.
examples.en: The tram goes there.

examples.de: Am Sonntag fahre ich ins Dorf, weil ich die Natur liebe.
examples.en: On Sunday I go to the village because I love nature.

examples.de: Ich finde, dass mein Viertel schön ist.
examples.en: I think that my neighbourhood is beautiful.

deeper.text: Notice how Mira starts each part with a different word: Ich, Hier, Es gibt, Am Samstag, Ich finde. A presentation sounds alive when the sentences do not all start with ich. Time words at the start are easy: the verb comes next, then the subject. And she ends with two short chunks that invite: Kommt mal vorbei! Ich wohne gern hier.

example.de: Am Samstag gehe ich auf den Marktplatz.
example.en: On Saturday I go to the market square.

cards.more: Think of a song with five short verses. Verse 1: Ich wohne in einem Vorort. Dorthin fährt die Straßenbahn. Verse 2: Hier wohnen viele Einwohner, aber es ist ruhig. Verse 3: Es gibt einen kleinen Marktplatz. Das Einkaufszentrum liegt am Stadtrand. Verse 4: Am Samstag gehe ich auf den Marktplatz. Am Sonntag fahre ich ins Dorf. Verse 5: Ich finde, dass mein Viertel schön ist. Kommt mal vorbei! Copy this song and change the places for your own town.
steps: 1 Ich wohne in einem Vorort. Dorthin fährt die Straßenbahn in zwanzig Minuten.
2 Hier wohnen viele Einwohner, aber es ist ruhig.
3 Es gibt einen kleinen Marktplatz. Das Einkaufszentrum liegt am Stadtrand und ein Dorf liegt in der Nähe.
4 Am Samstag gehe ich auf den Marktplatz. Am Sonntag fahre ich ins Dorf, weil ich die Natur liebe.
5 Ich finde, dass mein Viertel schön ist. Kommt mal vorbei! Ich wohne gern hier.

cards.title: Mira and Herr Ali: Wo wohnst du?
cards.body: Herr Ali asks Mira about her Viertel. He says du to Mira; Mira says Sie to him. Listen for the questions Wo? and Wohin? and for the answers: in einem Vorort (Wo?), dorthin and auf den Marktplatz (Wohin?).
cards.lead: You have practised the whole presentation. This card shows the short version in a real chat: a dialogue with Wo? and Wohin? questions and quick answers.

examples.de: Herr Ali fragt Mira.
examples.en: Herr Ali asks Mira.

examples.de: Wohin gehst du abends?
examples.en: Where do you go in the evening?

examples.de: Wohin gehen Sie?
examples.en: Where do you go? (formal)

deeper.text: In a chat you answer short: In einem Vorort instead of Ich wohne in einem Vorort. The case stays the same as in the full sentence, because the question still decides: Wo? gives the dative, Wohin? gives the accusative. So Wohin gehst du? → In den Park. Wo wohnst du? → Im Zentrum.

example.de: Wo wohnst du? Im Zentrum.
example.en: Where do you live? In the centre.

cards.more: Think of ping-pong: a question flies over, a short answer flies back. Wo wohnst du? In einem Vorort. Wohin gehst du abends? Auf den Marktplatz. The ball keeps its colour: a Wo? ball comes back as dative, a Wohin? ball as accusative. And remember who says what: Herr Ali says du to the young people, they say Sie to him. So Mira asks him: Und Sie? Wohin gehen Sie?
steps: Herr Ali: Wo wohnst du, Mira?
Mira: In einem Vorort. Dorthin fährt die Straßenbahn.
Herr Ali: Und wohin gehst du abends?
Mira: Ich gehe gern auf den Marktplatz. Und Sie? Wohin gehen Sie?
Herr Ali: Ins Restaurant „Zum Löwen“. Dort arbeite ich!
Mira: Dann komme ich mal vorbei!

lessons.title: Haustiere in Deutschland: react to information
lessons.goal: Talk about pets, pass on information with Ich habe gehört / gelesen, dass … and react to news.

grammar.topic: dass after hören, lesen, sehen and wissen; dass vs ob; reaction chunks; Wo? and Wohin? with animals
grammar.point: To pass on news say Ich habe gehört / gelesen / gesehen, dass … or Weißt du, dass …? and put the verb at the END of the dass-clause. Use ob instead of dass for an open yes/no question. React with Wirklich?, Echt?, Das habe ich nicht gewusst, Ich finde es toll, dass … or Schade, dass …
grammar.oneLine: Ich habe gehört, dass viele Deutsche eine Katze haben.

mistake.wrong: Ich habe gehört, dass viele Deutsche haben eine Katze.
mistake.right: Ich habe gehört, dass viele Deutsche eine Katze haben.
mistake.why: dass sends the conjugated verb (haben) to the very end of its clause, even when you pass on news.

terms.meaning: a part of a sentence that starts with dass (that); its verb goes to the end
whether: starts an open yes/no question inside a sentence
a short answer that shows what you feel about news: Wirklich? Echt?

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich finde es gut, dass …' to 'Ich habe gehört, dass …'
cards.body: Anna has read something about rabbits, and now she wants one. In real life you often pass on news: I have heard that …, I have read that …, Do you know that …? And the other person reacts: Really? I didn't know that! Today you learn both sides, with pets and Frau Weber's cat.
steps: You already know: dass with the verb at the end: Es stört mich, dass … and Wir haben entschieden, dass … (lessons 5 and 6), and Frau Weber's cat on the Fensterbrett (lesson 3).
New today: Ich habe gehört / gelesen / gesehen, dass … and Weißt du, dass …?, short reactions like Wirklich? and Echt?, and words for pets.
By the end you can: pass on information about pets, react to news and help the WG decide about an animal.

examples.de: Es stört mich, dass die Schuhe im Hausflur stehen.
examples.en: It bothers me that the shoes are standing in the hallway.
examples.why: You know this already: dass sends the verb to the end.

examples.de: Ich habe gehört, dass Frau Weber eine Katze hat.
examples.en: I have heard that Frau Weber has a cat.
examples.why: New today: dass after hören to pass on news.

cards.more: Think of news as a little parcel. You got it from somewhere: you heard it, read it or saw it. Now you hand it on: Ich habe gehört, dass … The parcel inside is a normal sentence, only its verb slides to the end, exactly like after Es stört mich, dass … The other person opens the parcel and reacts: Wirklich? Das habe ich nicht gewusst. You also learn the animals the parcel is about: der Hund, die Katze, das Kaninchen and der Vogel.

cards.title: Pets and what they do
cards.body: Das Tier is any animal; das Haustier lives with you. Der Hund bellt, die Katze sits on the Fensterbrett, das Kaninchen and der Vogel live in a Käfig (cage). You füttern (feed) them with Futter and you streicheln (stroke) them. A dog needs a Leine (lead) in the park.
cards.lead: You know das Haustier, der Hund, die Katze and der Fisch. This card adds more animals, what they do and where they are, with Wo? and Wohin?.

examples.de: Der Hund bellt.
examples.en: The dog barks.

examples.de: Die Katze sitzt auf dem Fensterbrett.
examples.en: The cat is sitting on the windowsill.

examples.de: Anna stellt den Käfig auf den Balkon.
examples.en: Anna puts the cage on the balcony.

deeper.text: Füttern and streicheln take an accusative object, like most verbs: Frau Weber füttert die Katze. Leon streichelt den Hund. And the Wo?/Wohin? rule works for animals too: the bird sits in the cage (Wo?, im Käfig), but Anna puts the cage on the balcony (Wohin?, auf den Balkon). Wo? → dative: Der Schrank steht in der Ecke. Wohin? → accusative: Ben stellt den Schrank in die Ecke.

example.de: Frau Weber füttert die Katze am Morgen.
example.en: Frau Weber feeds the cat in the morning.

cards.more: Think of a pet's day as three questions. What does it do? Der Hund bellt, die Katze schläft. Where is it? Das Kaninchen sitzt im Käfig, die Katze sitzt auf dem Fensterbrett (Wo?, dative). Where do we put it? Anna stellt den Käfig auf den Balkon (Wohin?, accusative). And what do you do for it? You füttern it with Futter and streicheln it. Say each line aloud with an animal you like.

cards.title: The Germans and their pets
cards.body: Many people in Germany have a Haustier, often a dog or a cat. In a rented flat the Vermieter (landlord) often has a say: look in the Mietvertrag. In many places a dog must be on a Leine. A Tierheim looks after animals without a home. And in a WG you ask the others first.
cards.lead: You know the animal words now. This card shows how people in Germany live with their pets, so you can compare it with your own country.

examples.de: Viele Deutsche haben ein Haustier.
examples.en: Many Germans have a pet.

examples.de: Im Park brauchen Hunde eine Leine.
examples.en: In the park dogs need a lead.

examples.de: Im Tierheim warten viele Tiere.
examples.en: Many animals are waiting in the animal shelter.

deeper.text: Why ask the Vermieter? In a rented flat an animal can bring noise or damage, so many contracts say what is allowed. A cat or a small bird is often fine, a big dog not always. Look at the Mietvertrag or ask. With an indirect question you can do it politely: Können Sie mir sagen, ob ich eine Katze haben darf?

example.de: Im Mietvertrag steht, ob man ein Tier haben darf.
example.en: The rental contract says whether you may have an animal.

cards.more: Think of a pet as a new flatmate. Before a new person moves in, you ask everybody. Before an animal moves in, you ask too: the Vermieter, the WG, maybe the neighbours. In Germany many people love their pets, but they also like rules: a dog at the Leine in the park, quiet at night. And if an animal has no home, it goes to a Tierheim. Now think: is it the same in your country? Fill the right column in your head.

rows: Viele Leute haben einen Hund oder eine Katze.
Im Mietvertrag steht, ob man ein Tier haben darf.
Ein Tierheim hilft Tieren ohne Familie.
In der WG fragt man zuerst die anderen.

cards.title: Pass on news with dass
cards.body: To pass on information, start with what you did: Ich habe gehört, …, Ich habe gelesen, …, Ich habe gesehen, … Then add a dass-clause with the verb at the END. To ask if someone knows a fact, say Weißt du, dass …? If you do not know the answer yourself, use ob.
cards.lead: You know dass after opinion words like Ich finde es gut. This card puts dass after hören, lesen, sehen and wissen, so you can pass on news.

examples.de: Ich habe gehört, dass viele Deutsche eine Katze haben.
examples.en: I have heard that many Germans have a cat.

examples.de: Ich habe gelesen, dass das Tierheim Hilfe braucht.
examples.en: I have read that the animal shelter needs help.

examples.de: Weißt du, dass Frau Weber eine Katze hat?
examples.en: Do you know that Frau Weber has a cat?

deeper.text: Dass and ob look alike but do different jobs. Dass carries a fact: you know it is true and you pass it on. Ob carries an open yes/no question: you do not know the answer. Weißt du, dass Frau Weber eine Katze hat? = I know it, do you? Weißt du, ob Frau Weber eine Katze hat? = I don't know, do you? In both, the verb goes to the end.

example.de: Weißt du, ob Frau Weber eine Katze hat?
example.en: Do you know whether Frau Weber has a cat?

cards.more: Think of two envelopes. The dass envelope holds a fact: Ich habe gesehen, dass die Katze auf dem Fensterbrett sitzt. The ob envelope holds a question mark: Ich weiß nicht, ob sie kommt. 1. Is it a fact you pass on? Use dass. 2. Is it a yes/no question you cannot answer? Use ob. 3. Push the verb to the end. A common mistake: Ich weiß nicht, dass sie kommt. You do not know, so it is a question: Ich weiß nicht, ob sie kommt.

…, dass Frau Weber eine Katze hat?
